title: Indian marks: silver makers' and retailers' marks of India, Burma and Ceylon, Indian hallmarks since 2000, origin stamps, and how Indian dates are written
applies_to: Marks and writing on items from India, Burma and Ceylon: the marks of colonial-era and regional silversmiths and retailers (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Kutch, Lucknow, Kashmir, Rangoon, Colombo), their pseudo-hallmarks, the Bureau of Indian Standards hallmarks on gold and silver, country and place stamps on export goods, and dates written in Indian eras, the Hijri year and regnal years in any Indian script's digits. A decode names what a mark names and gives the year a written date states; it never says an item is of the period, because marks were continued, shared and copied.

caveats: A mark names the maker, retailer or place it claims. Firms kept their marks for decades and successors continued them, so the dates are when a mark was used, not when an item was made.
Silver from Burma, Ceylon, China, the Straits and Siam is often sold in the West as Indian or Anglo-Indian. The marks help tell them apart; the style and making of the item matter as much.
Kutch silver is often said to be 95 to 98 percent silver. No source read gives a test for that figure; dealers’ acid tests report only that it is above 900.
reading: Silver made in India under British rule carries no assay office’s hallmark: India had no hallmarking system then. What it carries is a maker’s or retailer’s own mark, often a name or initials, sometimes with punches made to look like London’s hallmarks.
Read the marks in a row, as they were struck: initials or a name first, then any animals, heads or letters. A firm’s set of punches, not one punch alone, is what points to it.
A Roman letter beside an elephant or a lion on Calcutta silver is not a London date letter. Only Hamilton & Co., from 1937, struck a true yearly letter.
Regional silver from Kutch, Lucknow or Kashmir is often marked only with a maker’s initials and town (O.M. BHUJ), or not at all.

stamp_rules.name: US Tariff Act of 1890 (McKinley), sec. 6
stamp_rules.meaning: The rule behind country names on imports to the United States: from 1 March 1891, goods 'usually or ordinarily marked' had to carry the country of origin in legible English words.
stamp_rules.date_note: Act approved October 1890 (ch. 1244, 51st Congress); the marking clause took effect on 1 March 1891. Replaced by later tariff acts (1894, 1897, 1909, 1913, 1922, 1930), all of which kept a country-of-origin rule.
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: A country name such as INDIA on an item sold in the US points to export after 1 March 1891. It sets an earliest likely date for the mark, not for the item, and gives no latest date.
stamp_rules.cautions: The Act asked for the country of origin in English, not the words 'Made in'. It applied only to goods entering the US, so Indian items made for Britain, India itself or other markets were often never marked. Popular books date it to both 1890 (passage) and 1891 (effect).

facts.text: Section 6 of the Tariff Act of 1890 required that from 1 March 1891 foreign-made articles of a kind usually marked, and all packages of imports, be marked in legible English words to show the country of origin, or be refused entry.
facts.quote: on and after the first day of March, eighteen hundred and ninety-one, all articles of foreign manufacture ... shall ... be plainly marked, stamped, branded, or labeled in legible English words, so as to indicate the country of their origin

facts.text: Goods not so marked 'shall not be admitted to entry'.
facts.quote: and unless so marked, stamped, branded, or labeled they shall not be admitted to entry

facts.text: Collector references treat 1891 as the start of country names on export wares (for example ENGLAND on British pottery), while noting a few firms used a country name earlier.
facts.quote: With very few exceptions 'ENGLAND' was not used until 1891.

stamp_rules.name: US marking rule 1913-present: country of origin in English (Tariff Acts of 1913, 1922, 1930 sec. 304; 19 U.S.C. 1304; 19 CFR 134)
stamp_rules.meaning: Later US law kept the 1891 rule: imports must show the country of origin in English. Since 1938 the statute says 'the English name of the country of origin'. Abbreviations and variant spellings are allowed if unmistakable.
stamp_rules.date_note: 1913 Underwood Act superseded earlier marking clauses; 1922 Act; Tariff Act of 1930 sec. 304, rewritten by the Customs Administrative Act of 25 June 1938; current text 19 U.S.C. 1304 and 19 CFR Part 134.
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: Explains why Indian export goods for the US carry INDIA (or PAKISTAN, CEYLON, BURMA etc.) in English letters. None of these texts required the words 'Made in', so their presence or absence is not a legal date marker.
stamp_rules.cautions: Regional or city names (KASHMIR, BENARES, JAIPUR) are not country names; read with the current rule, such an item would also need INDIA to enter the US. No CBP ruling on 'Kashmir', 'Ceylon' or 'Burma' as marks was found.

facts.text: The 1913 tariff act required articles capable of being marked to be marked in legible English words so as to indicate the country of origin; it does not require 'Made in'.
facts.quote: in legible English words ... so as to indicate the country of origin

facts.text: The current statute (Tariff Act of 1930 sec. 304 as rewritten in 1938) requires marking that shows an ultimate purchaser in the United States the English name of the country of origin.
facts.quote: the English name of the country of origin of the article

facts.text: Customs regulations accept abbreviations that unmistakably indicate the country (e.g. 'Gt. Britain') and variant spellings that clearly indicate the English name (e.g. 'Brasil', 'Italie').
The marking provision passed from the 1913 act to the 1922 act and then to sec. 304 of the 1930 act.
facts.quote: superseding similar provisions of previous tariff acts

stamp_rules.name: When 'Made in' is actually required (19 CFR 134.46)
stamp_rules.meaning: Under current US customs rules the words 'Made in' or 'Product of' are required only when another place name (a US place, or a foreign country or locality other than the true origin) appears on the item and could mislead.
stamp_rules.date_note: Current regulation; the date it was first adopted was not established.
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: 'MADE IN INDIA' satisfies the rule but so does a bare 'INDIA'. The choice of wording was usually the maker's or importer's, so it cannot by itself date an item.
stamp_rules.cautions: Collector books often say 'Made in' became legally required in 1914, 1915, 1919 or 1921. No statute text found says so (see the 'made-in-india' row).

facts.text: 19 CFR 134.46 requires the country of origin to be preceded by 'Made in', 'Product of' or similar words only where 'United States', 'American', a US place, or a foreign country or locality other than the country of origin appears on the article and might mislead.
facts.quote: the name of the country of origin preceded by "Made in," "Product of," or other words of similar meaning.

facts.text: A collector reference states that the 'Made in' prefix was never a requirement of US import regulations or of the McKinley Act.
facts.quote: the "Made in" prefix was never a requirement of US import regulations or the McKinley Tariff Act itself.

stamp_rules.name: UK Merchandise Marks Act 1887, section 16
stamp_rules.meaning: British rule (in force from 1887): foreign goods bearing a British-looking name or trade mark had to carry a 'definite indication of the country in which the goods were made'. Goods without such names needed no origin mark.
stamp_rules.date_note: Act of 1887 (50 & 51 Vict. c. 28); superseded by the Trade Descriptions Act 1968.
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: Britain, the main market for Indian craft goods before 1947, did not require a country-of-origin mark on ordinary imports. Indian items sold in Britain are therefore often unmarked, and an unmarked item is not evidence of an early date.
stamp_rules.cautions: Whether goods from British India counted as 'foreign' under s.16 was not established. The Act is the source of the 'Made in Germany' style: commentators said a place name alone did not comply and a full statement such as 'manufactured in Germany' was needed.

facts.text: Section 16 barred the import of goods bearing the name or trade mark of a UK maker or trader unless accompanied by a definite indication of the country where the goods were made or produced.
facts.quote: a definite statement should be added

facts.text: In 1920 the Board of Trade told Parliament that goods without marks suggesting British origin did not need any indication of the country of manufacture on import.
facts.quote: Goods which do not bear marks suggestive of British origin are not required by the Merchandise Marks Act ... to bear on importation any indication of the country of manufacture.

facts.text: A contemporary legal commentary (Payn, 1888) gave 'manufactured in Germany' as the kind of statement that complied, and historians trace the 'Made in Germany' label to this British law.

stamp_rules.name: UK Merchandise Marks Act 1926: 'Empire' or 'Foreign' indications
stamp_rules.meaning: British rule: imported goods bearing British names, and classes of goods named in Orders in Council, had to bear an indication of origin, which could be the country's name or simply 'Empire' or 'Foreign'.
stamp_rules.date_note: Act 1926; first Orders in Council under s.2 from late 1927-1928 (draft laid 8 Nov 1927; six Orders covering 36 classes by 1929). Orders kept in force for three years after the Trade Descriptions Act 1968 took effect, so roughly to the early 1970s.
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: Explains marks reading EMPIRE or BRITISH EMPIRE on goods sold in Britain from the late 1920s; an Indian item for the British market could lawfully carry 'Empire' instead of 'India'.
stamp_rules.cautions: Orders covered only listed classes of goods (which ones covered Indian brass, textiles or rugs was not established). Even in 1938 there was no power to require marking of all imports or to require the country's name.

facts.text: The 1926 Act let imported goods be marked with a definite indication of the country of manufacture, or with 'Empire' or 'Foreign'.
facts.quote: the present option of marking "Empire" or "Foreign"

facts.text: In 1938 the government said the Act gave no power to require all imported goods to be marked, nor to insist that the indication be the country's name.
facts.quote: There is no power under that Act either to require all imported goods to be marked

facts.text: No Order in Council had been made under s.2 by 16 November 1927 (a draft was laid on 8 November 1927); by 1929 six Orders covered 36 classes of goods.
The Trade Descriptions Act 1968 s.42 kept s.2 Orders in force for three years after that Act took effect.

stamp_rules.name: Indian Merchandise Marks Act 1889 (Act IV of 1889)
stamp_rules.meaning: British India's law on false trade descriptions, including false statements of the place or country where goods were made. It governed what an Indian maker could truthfully stamp; it did not require export goods to be marked.
stamp_rules.date_note: Act IV of 1889; repealed in India by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act 1958 (Act 43 of 1958) with effect from 25 November 1959. Still in force in Bangladesh (and, per search excerpts, Pakistan).
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: A false 'MADE IN INDIA' or false place name was an offence in British India, but no Indian rule requiring origin stamps on exports was found. Indian export marks were driven by the importing country's law.
stamp_rules.cautions: No Indian export-marking requirement for handicrafts in the 1880s-1990s was found; see gaps.

facts.text: The Act defines 'trade description' to include any indication of the place or country in which, or the time at which, goods were made or produced.
facts.quote: (b) as to the place or country in which, or the time at which, any goods were made or produced

facts.text: The Act was repealed in India by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act 1958 (Act 43 of 1958), s.136, with effect from 25 November 1959.

stamp_rules.name: US Textile Fiber Products Identification Act: country of origin on textile labels
stamp_rules.meaning: From 3 March 1960, imported textile products sold in the US (including rugs) had to carry a label naming the country where processed or manufactured, with fiber content.
stamp_rules.date_note: Act of 2 September 1958 (Pub. L. 85-897), effective 3 March 1960. Extended to US-made goods by Pub. L. 98-417 (1984).
stamp_rules.what_it_tells: A sewn fabric label giving fiber content plus 'MADE IN INDIA' on a textile or rug sold in the US fits the post-1960 labeling regime.
stamp_rules.cautions: The label can be removed or added; older textiles were sometimes relabeled by later sellers. Wool Products Labeling Act rules differ and exempt carpets.

facts.text: Section 70b(b)(4) requires an imported textile fiber product to be labeled with the name of the country where it was processed or manufactured.
facts.quote: If it is an imported textile fiber product the name of the country where processed or manufactured.

facts.text: The Act was approved 2 September 1958 and took effect 3 March 1960.
facts.quote: the law will become effective on March 3, 1960

facts.text: Carpets, rugs and mats are covered by the Textile Act; the Wool Act exempts carpets.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of John Mair, jeweler, silversmith and medallist, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: As illustrated on 925-1000.com: a thistle, I.M, and a punch showing a key (one example only)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Working years in Calcutta as given by 925-1000.com from Wilkinson 1987; Mair lived 1759-1815.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Calcutta work of c.1789-1796, among the earliest marked European-style silver made in India.
rows.cautions: The thistle and key punches look like Scottish marks; early silver of this kind was long catalogued as Scottish provincial (see the thistle row). Only one illustrated example found.

facts.text: John Mair (1759-1815) worked in Calcutta 1789-1796 as jeweler, silversmith and medallist; in 1793 he cut the dies for and struck about 7,000 gold and silver medals for the Mysore campaign.
facts.quote: In 1793, Mair cut the dies and struck approx. 7,000 gold & silver medals awarded by the East India Company to British troops for service in the Mysore Campaign.

facts.text: 925-1000.com illustrates his mark as I.M between a thistle and a key-shaped punch.
Calcutta silversmiths, lacking an assay office, used pseudo marks such as lions, anchors, keys and thistles.
facts.quote: Without an assay office system in India, silversmiths used pseudo marks, icons such as lions, anchors, keys, and thistles.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Hippolitus Poignand, silversmith, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Star (or flower) device + HP + a sovereign's (king's) head + small tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Arrived Calcutta 1793; died there 19 May 1805.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1793-1805. A head punch here imitates the British sovereign's-head duty mark; it is not a British duty mark.
rows.cautions: The king's head and star can be read as British or Scottish marks. A similar star device was used by Joseph Rondo, who bought Poignand's remaining stock after his death (925-1000 forum).

facts.text: Poignand worked in Calcutta 1793-1805 at successive addresses: 1793 Mr Charles' Europe Shop; 1794 13 Bankshall St; 1798 4 Tank Square; 1800 51 Theatre St; 1805 191 Lall Bazar.
Born in Jersey 29 August 1761, arrived Calcutta 1793, died there 19 May 1805.
facts.quote: Hippolitus Poignand died in Calcutta on the 19th May 1805.

facts.text: A salver of c.1800 is 'Marked underneath with HP, King's head mark, and tally mark.'
facts.quote: Marked underneath with HP, King's head mark, and tally mark.

facts.text: His 'star' device is similar to one used by Joseph Rondo of Calcutta, who bought Poignand's remaining stock.
facts.quote: The 'star' device shown above is similar to one used by another Calcutta silversmith of this period, Joseph Rondo

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of John Hunt / John Hunt & Co., jewelers and silversmiths, 51 Theatre Street, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: 925-1000.com illustrates JH with a fouled anchor and letter punches (one example)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Firm dates from 925-1000.com (after Wilkinson 1987); a saucepan by John Hunt is dated c.1810 by Dreweatts.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, c.1808-1815. Succeeded by Francis Dormieux & Co.; W. H. Twentyman trained here.
rows.cautions: Anchor punches on Calcutta silver were once read as the Greenock town mark. Exact punch sequence not confirmed by a second source.

facts.text: John Hunt & Co., 51 Theatre St, Calcutta, 1808-1815: John Hunt and Thomas Thompson; Thompson replaced by Charles Dolton in 1812; succeeded by Dormieux & Co.
William Henry Twentyman arrived in Calcutta in 1810 and was apprenticed to his uncle John Hunt for five years.
facts.quote: Arriving in Calcutta in 1810, William was apprentice to his uncle John Hunt for five years.

facts.text: Dreweatts offered 'An Indian Colonial silver saucepan and lid, John Hunt, circa 1810'.

rows.meaning: Mark of Francis Dormieux & Co., engraver, jeweler and retailer, 51 Theatre Street, Calcutta
rows.device: initials F and D separated by a pellet
rows.punch_set: Worn mark possibly in an Indian script + thistle (octagonal punch) + year in figures (e.g. 1813, 1816) + uncrowned leopard's head + F.D
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Firm dates 1815-1821 (925-1000.com after Wilkinson 1987); items carry year punches 1813 (925-1000 photo) and 1816 (V&A salver), so Dormieux was marking before the firm date given.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1813-1821. The year in figures is part of the maker's own punch set, so it probably gives the year of making, but it is not an assay date letter.
rows.cautions: Leopard's head imitates the London town mark and the thistle the Edinburgh standard mark: read together they can be mistaken for British hallmarks. Successor to John Hunt & Co.

facts.text: Dormieux's Calcutta mark set combines F.D with an uncrowned leopard's head and a year in figures.
Francis Dormieux & Co., 51 Theatre St, Calcutta, 1815-1821: Francis Dormieux and Francis Vrignon, successors to John Hunt & Co.

V&A salver M.103-1940 is punched, left to right: a worn mark in a shaped punch (?Sanskrit script), a thistle in an octagonal punch, the date-mark 1816, an uncrowned leopard's head, and FD separated by a pellet.
facts.quote: thistle mark in octagonal punch; the date-mark '1816' in a rectangular punch (worn); a leopard's head uncrowned (worn); the initials 'FD' separated by a pellet

facts.text: 925-1000.com illustrates a set reading 1813, a leopard's head and F.D.
Dormieux is described by the V&A as engraver and retailer.
facts.quote: the mark of the engraver and retailer Francis Dormieux & Co.

facts.text: Dessert spoons by F. Dormieux were in the Fiona Buchanan collection.

rows.meaning: Personal mark of Robert Hamilton, founder of Hamilton & Co., Calcutta, before the firm style H&Co
rows.punch_set: Elephant + Roman capital A + RH (per ASCAS after Wilkinson 1987); RH alone on a gold snuff box
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Hamilton set up at 5 Tank Square in 1808 and ceased to have an interest in the firm in 1817; Chiswick dates his RH mark 1808-13.
rows.what_it_tells: Very early Hamilton work, c.1808-1813/17. The elephant and A continued under the firm mark H&Co.
rows.cautions: RH is a common British maker's initial pair; without the elephant/A it cannot be told from a British maker's mark.

facts.text: Before the firm became Hamilton & Co., its marks were an elephant, a capital A and Robert Hamilton's initials R H.
facts.quote: Before Hamilton & Co. foundation the marks were an elephant, a capital letter A and the Robert Hamilton initials (R H)

facts.text: A gold snuff box, Calcutta c.1810, bears 'maker's mark RH only'; catalogued as Robert Hamilton (active 1808-17, mark used 1808-13).
facts.quote: The interior with maker's mark RH only.

facts.text: Robert Hamilton (1772-1848) arrived in Calcutta in 1808 and opened at 5 Tank Square under license from the East India Company.
facts.quote: established in Calcutta by Robert Hamilton under licence from the East India Company.

facts.text: Hamilton trained in Edinburgh under William Cunningham I.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Hamilton & Co., jewelers and silversmiths, Old Court House Street, Calcutta, struck with the firm's elephant and Roman A
rows.device: letters H&Co (often read H&C); with an elephant punch
rows.punch_set: H&Co + elephant + Roman capital A; on better items c.1815-1850 also an urn ('cup and cover'); c.1812-1820 a 'tailed sphere', then c.1821-1860 a thistle; plus a small incuse tally mark (lotus, crescent, trefoil, pellet, pelleted square, trident)

maker.name: Hamilton & Co.
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata); branches Bombay (1833-36 and from 1868), Simla and Delhi (from 1865)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.where_on_object: underside or foot rim; on flatware the back of the stem
rows.date_note: Firm mark from the 1811 partnership; the urn and thistle variants are dated by ASCAS (after Wilkinson) to c.1812-1860; the author calls these ranges estimates. Dated items: entree dishes 1813, covered cup 1837, standing cup 1867.
rows.what_it_tells: Made (or at least marked) by Hamilton & Co. in Calcutta, the largest and longest-lived European silversmiths in India. The extra punches narrow the date only roughly.
rows.cautions: Not British hallmarks: there is no town mark, no sovereign's head and the A is not a date letter. The elephant was long mistaken for an Inverness town mark (Jackson 1921 still listed a Hamilton strainer among Inverness marks). Pittar & Co. and Charles, Nephew & Co. also used a Roman A, and J. Boseck & Co. an elephant. Hamilton imported British silver too, so a British-hallmarked item with a Hamilton name may be English-made.

facts.text: Robert Hamilton set up in Calcutta in 1808, took Henry and James Glazbrook as partners in 1811 and ceased to have an interest in 1817; the firm kept his name through many later partnerships.
facts.quote: He enters into partnership with Henry Glazbrook (who had arrived in 1810) and James Glazbrook (who had arrived in 1811) in 1811

facts.text: Marks c.1812-1820: H & Co with an elephant and A, accompanied by an urn and a 'tailed sphere'; c.1821-1845 the elephant and urn in shaped punches with the A and a thistle(?); c.1850-1860 the urn dropped but the thistle continued.
facts.quote: The elephant and the urn are struck in punches which follow the borders of the symbols and the letter 'A'. A new symbol (a thistle ?) is now struck instead of the tailed sphere

facts.text: The urn mark tends to appear on more important items and was used c.1815-1850 (Wilkinson 1999, p.53, as cited).
facts.quote: the urn mark tends to have only appeared on more important pieces and was used from 1815 to 1850.

facts.text: Catalogued examples: entree dishes dated 1813 marked H&Co, elephant, Roman capital A and an incuse trefoil tally mark; curry pans c.1830-50 marked H&Co, an elephant, a cup and cover, Roman capital A.
facts.quote: Marked underneath only with H&Co, an elephant, a cup and cover, Roman capital A

facts.text: V&A caster M.180&A-1922 (c.1810) is marked on the bottom 'H and Co', an animal (elephant?) and the letter A.
facts.quote: Bottom: “H and Co” for Hamilton & Co., animal (elephant?), letter A

facts.text: In a letter of 5 March 1919 the firm stated that for over a hundred years its mark had been H. & Co. with an elephant.
facts.quote: their mark for over a hundred years had been H. & Co. with an elephant

facts.text: Hamilton's marks were long confused with Scottish ones: early publications put them under Inverness because the elephant was taken for an Inverness town mark.
facts.quote: In early publications they are often seen in the Inverness section as the elephant punch was mistaken for an Inverness town mark.

facts.text: Address: 7 Old Court House Street from 1809/1811 (ASCAS; forum; Wilkinson 1999 p.53 via Backman); 925-1000.com gives 8 Old Court House St.

rows.plain: H and Co (Hamilton and Company), later marks
rows.meaning: Hamilton & Co., Calcutta, marks of c.1860-1937: firm initials and elephant, with or without A, later with SILVER or STERLING SILVER
rows.punch_set: H&Co + elephant + A (+ tally mark), often with the name stamp HAMILTON & CO JEWELLERS CALCUTTA; from c.1914 H&Co + elephant + SILVER or STERLING SILVER, A usually omitted; Bombay-branch items from 1868 lack the A

maker.name: Hamilton & Co.
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata); branches Bombay (1833-36 and from 1868), Simla and Delhi (from 1865)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: ASCAS gives c.1860-1914 (estimate) for H&Co, elephant and A without thistle; SILVER from at least 1914; H&Co Ltd after 1926. Chiswick dates H&Co L + elephant + A + STERLING SILVER wine labels to c.1910, which conflicts with ASCAS's post-1926 Ltd.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta (or Bombay branch) work of the later 19th and early 20th century. 'SILVER'/'STERLING SILVER' is the firm's own claim, not an assay.
rows.cautions: An A-less mark may be Bombay-branch work after 1868 or post-1914 Calcutta work. The elephant also appears with JB&Co (J. Boseck & Co.).

facts.text: In the early 20th century Hamilton & Co. struck H&Co with the elephant and the word SILVER.
From 1868 marks struck on items made at the Bombay branch lack the A.
facts.quote: Since this date, on marks struck on items crafted at the Bombay branch, the A is missing.

facts.text: Bombay branch 1833-36 and from 1868; Delhi and Simla from 1865 (ASCAS). Lyon & Turnbull gives Bombay opened 1830 and Simla 1865.
The word SILVER was struck at least from 1914, usually without the A.
facts.quote: The mark is without the capital A and bears the word 'silver' which was then struck at least from this date on

facts.text: Catalogued examples: H&Co, elephant, Roman capital A and crescent tally mark, also stamped HAMILTON & CO JEWELLERS CALCUTTA (c.1850-1870); salt spoons c.1910 marked H&Co, SILVER and the elephant.
facts.quote: Each marked with H&Co, SILVER and the elephant.

facts.text: Wine labels c.1900 bear the retailer's marks H&Co, an elephant and the word SILVER.
facts.quote: The retailer’s marks: ‘H&Co’, an elephant and the word ‘SILVER’ are impressed on the underside of each label.

facts.text: A Hamilton huqqa bought at the Paris Exhibition of 1867 (V&A) bears pseudo-assay marks of an elephant and the letter 'P' in Bengali script.
facts.quote: Pseudo-assay marks of an elephant and 'P' in Bengali script on the cover of the 'chilim' (tobacco bowl).

rows.plain: H and Co Limited (Hamilton and Company Limited)
rows.meaning: Hamilton & Co. Ltd., Calcutta: firm mark in a three-lobed punch with the elephant and a yearly date letter (from 1937)
rows.device: letters H&Co Ld in a trefoil (three-lobed) punch; elephant
rows.punch_set: H&Co Ld (trefoil) + elephant + date letter + SILVER or STERLING SILVER

maker.name: Hamilton & Co.
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata); branches Bombay (1833-36 and from 1868), Simla and Delhi (from 1865)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Date letters from 1937: A 1937, B 1938, C 1939, D 1940, E 1941, F 1942, G 1943, H 1944, I 1945, K 1946, L 1947, M 1948, N 1949 ... Z 1961 (J omitted), then A again 1962 ... M 1973 when the firm closed (ASCAS, source given as Wilkinson). The trefoil shape is recorded at least from 1954.
rows.what_it_tells: This is the only Indian colonial firm found with a true yearly date letter. Letters A-M are ambiguous between 1937-48 and 1962-73; use style and any inscription to choose.
rows.cautions: Do not read the letter with a British date-letter table. Closing date disputed: 1970 (V&A, 'until 30 June 1970'), 1971 (925-1000; Lyon & Turnbull), 1973 (ASCAS; 925-1000 forum). Sources read do not show whether letters N-Z were reused after 1961 other than the restart at A in 1962.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co. struck a yearly date letter from 1937; letter G corresponds to 1943, matching a set of dishes engraved 1.4.44.
From 1937 a date letter replaced the traditional Roman A, running through 25 letters (J omitted) and restarting with A in 1962; the series ran until the firm closed in 1973.
facts.quote: From 1937 a date letter was introduced in place of the traditional Roman 'A'. The series ran until H & Co Ltd. closed in 1973, with 25 letters of the Roman Alphabet (leaving out the 'J')

facts.text: A set of dishes catalogued 'Calcutta 1943 by Hamilton and Co' is 'marked to the side and with date letter G' and engraved 'Rafpol 1.4.44', consistent with G = 1943.
facts.quote: Each marked to the side and with date letter G.

facts.text: A pair of salvers 'probably 1940' is marked H&Co, elephant, date letter D, and STERLING SILVER.
facts.quote: Each marked to the reverse H&Co, elephant, date letter D, and STERLING SILVER.

facts.text: The Ltd mark took its characteristic three-lobed shape at least from 1954, probably earlier.
facts.quote: At least from this date on, but probably earlier, the maker's mark of Hamilton & Co Ltd assumed the characteristic tri-lobed shape

facts.text: V&A states the firm traded continuously until 30 June 1970.
facts.quote: traded continuously until 30 June 1970.

rows.meaning: Name stamp of Hamilton & Co., Calcutta (retail/firm stamp), used with or instead of the pseudo-hallmarks
rows.punch_set: Struck alongside H&Co + elephant + A + tally (mid-19th century), or alone (e.g. 1926 trophy; 1947 presentation item)

maker.name: Hamilton & Co.
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata); branches Bombay (1833-36 and from 1868), Simla and Delhi (from 1865)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Seen on items catalogued c.1850-1870 with the full pseudo set; 'Hamilton & Co. Calcutta' alone on a trophy inscribed 1926; 'HAMILTONS CALCUTTA' on an item presented 22 April 1947.
rows.what_it_tells: Confirms Hamilton & Co. as maker or seller; on its own it does not prove the item was made in India.
rows.cautions: A name stamp can be added by a retailer to bought-in work; Hamilton imported British silver (Rundell, Bridge & Rundell) and was called the largest importer of British silver into India.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co. also stamped its name with CALCUTTA on silver.
Catalogued as 'also stamped HAMILTON & CO JEWELLERS CALCUTTA' alongside H&Co, elephant, A and tally mark.
facts.quote: also stamped HAMILTON & CO JEWELLERS CALCUTTA.

facts.text: A trophy cup inscribed 1926 bears 'Hamilton & Co. Calcutta' instead of the usual trade mark.
facts.quote: There is not the traditional trade mark, but the impression 'Hamilton & Co. Calcutta'

facts.text: 925-1000.com illustrates a two-line stamp HAMILTON & Co / CALCUTTA.
A 1947 presentation model boat is 'Stamped to the side HAMILTONS CALCUTTA.'
facts.quote: Stamped to the side HAMILTONS CALCUTTA.

rows.plain: Hamilton and Co on British-hallmarked silver
rows.meaning: Hamilton & Co. of Calcutta as sponsor or retailer of silver assayed in Britain
rows.punch_set: H&Co (or the firm name) with full British hallmarks (town mark, lion passant, date letter)

maker.name: Hamilton & Co.
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata); branches Bombay (1833-36 and from 1868), Simla and Delhi (from 1865)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Imports recorded from Rundell, Bridge & Rundell (1820s); a London-hallmarked 1910 box is catalogued 'by Hamilton and Co of Calcutta'. Culme (oral) records the maker's mark still H & Co in 1912.
rows.what_it_tells: The item was assayed in Britain and was probably made there; Hamilton was the Indian seller.
rows.cautions: Say so to the owner: such an item is English-made silver retailed in India, not Indian colonial silver.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co. imported British-made silver to be sold in India.
Hamilton & Co. is recorded importing items from Rundell, Bridge & Rundell in London.
facts.quote: recorded importing items from Rundell Bridge & Rundell in London

facts.text: The V&A describes Hamilton and Company as 'the largest importer of British silver into India'.
facts.quote: the largest importer of British silver into India.

facts.text: A sterling silver miniature playing-cards box, London 1910, is catalogued 'by Hamilton and Co of Calcutta'.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Middleton & Co., Calcutta, struck with imitation Edinburgh castle and thistle marks
rows.punch_set: M&Co. + imitation castle (Edinburgh town mark) + imitation thistle (Edinburgh standard mark)

maker.name: Middleton & Co. (Robert Brutus Middleton and Thomas Allardyce)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Partnership years given by the V&A.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1822-1834. One of the clearest cases of a Calcutta firm imitating a British assay office (Edinburgh).
rows.cautions: Easily read as Edinburgh hallmarks; check for the missing date letter and the M&Co. initials. Middleton had worked for Hamilton & Co. (ASCAS lists a James Middleton among Hamilton partners; relation unclear).

facts.text: V&A mug M.847-1926 is marked 'M&Co.' for Middleton & Co. of Calcutta with imitations of the castle and thistle marks of the Edinburgh Assay Office.
facts.quote: Marked on the base: ‘M&Co.’ for Middleton & Co of Calcutta., and with imitations of the castle and thistle marks of the Edinburgh Assay Office.

facts.text: Robert Brutus Middleton and Thomas Allardyce were partners in Middleton and Co. 1822-1834; Middleton had been an assistant at Hamilton and Company.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of William Henry Twentyman, silversmith, Calcutta, working alone
rows.punch_set: WHT + crescent and star + fouled anchor + tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Chiswick dates the WHT mark to his years working alone, 1815-1821; he set up in 1815 after five years with his uncle John Hunt and retired in 1842.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, c.1815-1821.
rows.cautions: The anchor led early catalogues to attribute 'unknown WHT' to Greenock, Scotland. The crescent and star is not a Turkish or Ottoman mark here.

facts.text: W. H. Twentyman's Calcutta marks include his initials WHT struck with a fouled anchor.
An egg cruet c.1820 is 'Marked to the foot edge WHT, a crescent and star, a fouled anchor, and a tally mark.'
facts.quote: Marked to the foot edge WHT, a crescent and star, a fouled anchor, and a tally mark.

facts.text: Work by the 'unknown WHT' was attributed to Greenock in early exhibitions, books and sale catalogues, presumably because of the anchor mark.
facts.quote: work by the ‘unknown WHT’ was attributed to Greenock, presumably due to the use of an anchor mark on many of his pieces.

facts.text: Twentyman arrived in Calcutta in 1810, apprenticed to his uncle John Hunt for five years, set up in 1815 and worked at Tank Square and Hare Street until retiring in 1842.
facts.quote: He set up on his own immediately leaving the employ of his Master in 1815 and worked at Tank Square and Hare Street until 1842.

facts.text: William Henry Twentyman is named among the makers of Fiddle-pattern flatware c.1830.

rows.plain: T B and Co (Twentyman, Beck and Company)
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Twentyman, Beck & Co., Calcutta, with the East India Company lion crest
rows.punch_set: TB&Co + lion rampant holding a crown (East India Company crest) + crowned lion passant (or lion passant) + tally mark (e.g. a number)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Partnership years 1821-23 as catalogued by Sotheby's and Chiswick (after Wilkinson 1973).
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1821-1823; the crowned lion passant is recorded by Wilkinson only for this firm.
rows.cautions: The lion rampant is not a Scottish or Dutch mark here: Wilkinson reads it as the East India Company crest, perhaps used like a royal warrant.

facts.text: Twentyman, Beck & Co. (1821-23) marked TB&Co with a lion rampant and a (crowned) lion passant.
A silver-gilt jar is 'marked on base with tally mark 22, crowned lion passant, makers mark, and lion rampant holding crown'.
facts.quote: marked on base with tally mark 22, crowned lion passant, makers mark, and lion rampant holding crown

facts.text: Wilkinson (1973, p.155): the lion rampant reproduces the crest of the East India Company and may have been used like a royal warrant; the crowned lion passant was noted only with this firm. (quoted in Sotheby's 2013 catalogue)
facts.quote: The lion rampant mark is a reproduction of the crest of the East India Company, and may have been used in very much the same way as a Royal warrant is used today

facts.text: Peppers and a curry-pan stand, Calcutta 1821-23, are marked TB&Co, lion rampant, lion passant and tally mark.
facts.quote: Each marked underneath with TB&Co, lion rampant, lion passant, and tally mark.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Twentyman & Co., silversmiths, 3 Tank Square and later 3 Hare Street, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: T&Co (gothic) + lion passant + tally mark (annulet, crossed square, three dots in a row)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.where_on_object: underside or foot rim; back of flatware stems
rows.date_note: Chiswick: active 1818-20, then 1824-53; Backman (after Wilkinson 1999): first mentioned 1821, last 1854; 925-1000.com: 1818-1829. 3 Tank Square until 1836, then 3 Hare Street.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, c.1824-1853; one of the most important Calcutta firms of the period.
rows.cautions: The gothic T&Co is easily read as a British maker's mark; with only a lion passant and a tally mark it lacks a town mark and date letter. Jackson 1921 lists a 'T. & Co.' among Inverness marks (table forks) - possibly this firm, not confirmed.

facts.text: Twentyman & Co. marked T&Co in gothic letters with a lion passant and a tally mark.

A teapot base is marked T&Co in Gothic lettering for Twentyman & Company, a lion passant and a tally mark of three punch marks in a row; the firm is first mentioned in 1821 and last in 1854 (Wilkinson 1999). [dates are Wilkinson 1999 as cited by Backman; mark observation is Backman's]
facts.quote: The base is marked with a maker’s mark of T&Co in Gothic lettering for Twentyman & Company, a lion passant mark and a tally mark of three punch marks in a row.

facts.text: Chiswick lots: 'Marked underneath T&Co, lion passant and an annulet tally mark'; a 'toffee' pot marked 'T&Co, pseudo lion passant and tally mark'; a milk ladle with maker's mark 'Wilkinson B.52.3'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath T&Co, lion passant and an annulet tally mark.

facts.text: Twentyman and Co worked from 3 Tank Square until 1836, thereafter 3 Hare Street (Wilkinson 1987).
facts.quote: working from 3 Tank Square until 1836, thereafter 3 Hare Street.

facts.text: Partners per 925-1000.com: William Henry Twentyman and George Havell Homser [Hosmer, who ran the watchmaking per L&T].

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Edward Cropley & Co., jewelers and goldsmiths, Old Court House Street, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: C&Co + lion passant + capital B
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Established 1819; partnership with Charles Dolton dissolved 31 Dec 1823; Cropley left Calcutta in 1825.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1819-c.1825. Cropley had been a London manufacturer (Frith Street, Soho), probably supplying Rundell, Bridge & Rundell.
rows.cautions: The lion passant imitates the English sterling mark (V&A notes this was illegal in England). 'C&Co' alone is a common initials mark; the B and lion passant together point to Calcutta.

facts.text: Cropley & Co., Calcutta (from 1819), marked C&Co with a lion passant and a capital B.
V&A sugar casters M.155-1940 are marked C&Co. and simulated hallmarks, with the letter B; Cropley mainly used the B mark and a simulated sterling lion passant.
facts.quote: Cropley mainly used the 'B' mark. This caster is also punched with a simulated sterling mark, the lion passant, a practice illegal in England.

facts.text: A beaker c.1820 is 'Marked to underside, with C&Co, lion passant, and a capital B.'
facts.quote: Marked to underside, with C&Co, lion passant, and a capital B.

facts.text: Edward Cropley established Cropley and Co. in Calcutta in 1819, advertising that he had been for 15 years principal manufacturer to the first houses in London.
facts.quote: Edward Cropley was for 15 years principal manufacturer to the first houses in London

facts.text: 925-1000.com dates the firm 1819-1825 at Old Court House St; partners possibly James Pembroke Cropley, Thomas Thompson and/or Charles Dolton.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Pittar & Co., jewelers and silversmiths, 9 Old Court House Street, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: P&Co + lion passant + Roman capital A (+ tally mark; sometimes a journeyman's mark)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: 1825-1848 (925-1000.com, Chiswick, after Wilkinson); the V&A says several partnerships 1825-1840; Backman 1831-1848.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, c.1825-1848. Succeeded by Charles, Nephew & Co.
rows.cautions: The Roman A also appears on Hamilton & Co. silver (the V&A suggests Robert Hamilton was probably an early Pittar partner); P&Co is also a common British initials mark. Not to be confused with John Pittar of Dublin (18th century).

facts.text: Pittar & Co., Calcutta, marked P&Co with a lion passant and a Roman capital A.
Curry pan c.1830 'Marked underneath with P & Co, pseudo lion passant, and capital A'; flatware 'marked with incuse makers mark, pseudo lion passant and capital A, and tally mark'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath with P & Co, pseudo lion passant, and capital A.

facts.text: V&A casters M.201-1923 are marked P&Co., A and a simulated sterling mark; one early partner was probably Robert Hamilton, who used a similar Roman A.
facts.quote: One of the early partners was probably Robert Hamilton of Hamilton and Co. who adopted a similar Roman 'A' mark

facts.text: A cup's foot rim is punched P&Co, a lion passant, the letter A and two smaller marks.
facts.quote: The rim of the foot is punched with the maker’s mark stamp of ‘P&Co’, a lion passant, the letter ‘A’, and two smaller marks.

facts.text: Partners: Parke Pittar I, Isaac Pittar and (probably) Robert Hamilton; 9 Old Court House St; succeeded by Charles, Nephew & Co.
A mug of 1832 is inscribed 'Pittar and Co. Old Court Street, Calcutta'.
Jackson (1921) records the 'Mark of Pittar [OCR: Pillar] & Co. of Calcutta: per Messrs. Bruford.'

rows.plain: A P L and Co (Arthur Pittar, Lattey and Company)
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Arthur Pittar, Lattey & Co., Calcutta
rows.punch_set: APL&Co + lion passant + Roman capital B + tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Partnership founded 1835 by Arthur Pittar and Robert John Lattey; John Pittar and Arthur Pittar Lattey joined 1840; continued as Lattey Brothers & Co. from 1842.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1835-1842.
rows.cautions: Lyon & Turnbull catalogued a mug 'MARKED AF, LION PASSANT B' as Pittar, Lattey & Co.; AF is probably a misreading of a worn APL punch (unconfirmed). Dreweatts dates a 'Lattey Brothers & Co.' item 1835-1840, i.e. within the Pittar, Lattey years.

facts.text: Pittar, Lattey & Co. (1835-42) items carry a lion passant and a capital B.
Fruit eaters c.1840 'Each marked with APL&Co, pseudo lion passant, capital Roman B, tally mark.'
facts.quote: Each marked with APL&Co, pseudo lion passant, capital Roman B, tally mark.

facts.text: Pittar, Lattey & Co. was founded in 1835 by Arthur Pittar (in Calcutta since 1821) and Robert John Lattey (his assistant since 1828); continued as Lattey Brothers & Co. from 1842.
facts.quote: The firm of Pittar, Lattey & Co of Calcutta was a partnership founded in 1835 by Arthur Pittar

facts.text: A christening mug catalogued as Pittar, Lattey & Co. is 'MARKED AF, LION PASSANT B'.

rows.plain: L B and Co (Lattey Brothers and Company)
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Lattey Brothers & Co., jewelers and silversmiths, 10 Government Place, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Either LB&Co + lion passant + capital B (+ G) + annulet or crescent tally; or LB / LB&Co + fouled anchor + lion passant + gothic L (or I) + crown + pellet tally
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: 1842/43-1855 (Chiswick 'active 1843-55'; L&T 'formed in 1842'; 925-1000.com 1842-1855); succeeded by Allan & Hayes.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, 1842-1855. Two different pseudo sets are recorded; the reason (date or workshop) is not explained in the sources read.
rows.cautions: The anchor, crown and gothic letter make this set look like a British (Birmingham/Sheffield-type) hallmark; the gothic letter is not a date letter.

facts.text: Lattey Brothers & Co. marked LB&Co with a lion passant and a capital B (other sets add a fouled anchor, gothic letter and crown).

Cruets c.1855 'Each marked underneath with LB, fouled anchor, lion passant, gothic L, crown, and a tally mark'; a ewer c.1850 'LB&Co, fouled anchor, lion passant, gothic I, crown, and pellet tally mark'.
facts.quote: Each marked underneath with LB, fouled anchor, lion passant, gothic L, crown, and a tally mark.

facts.text: Tablespoons 1850 'Each marked with LB&Co, a lion passant and a capital B, and an annulet tally mark'; a curry pan 'LB&Co, lion passant, B, and G'.
facts.quote: Each marked with LB&Co, a lion passant and a capital B, and an annulet tally mark.

facts.text: 925-1000.com illustrates LB&Co with a lion passant, a B and a crescent.

Lattey Brothers (R.J. Lattey, A.P. Lattey, D. Lattey and Joseph Hayes), 10 Government Place, worked 1842/43-1855 and were succeeded by Allan & Hayes; a pap feeder is illustrated in Wilkinson 1973, p.86, A108.1.
facts.quote: Lattey Brothers were formed in 1842, from the earlier firm of Pittar Lattey & Co, and continued until they were succeeded in 1855 by Allan & Hayes.

rows.meaning: Name mark of Allan & Hayes, jewelers and silversmiths, 10 Government Place, Calcutta (successors to Lattey Brothers)
rows.punch_set: ALLAN & HAYES (or ALLAN&HAYES) + crescent tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Chiswick: first mentioned 1856, dissolved 1867; 925-1000.com: successors to Lattey Brothers in 1855. A London Gazette notice of 1867 concerns the insolvency of partner Dugald Lattey.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, c.1855-1867. No pseudo-hallmarks: the firm used its full name with a tally mark.
rows.cautions: Allan & Hayes was run by the Lattey family and R. T. Callan (no Allan or Hayes named in the 1867 notice). Successor: Callan & Co. (mark not found).

facts.text: Allan & Hayes were jewelers at 10 Government Place, Calcutta, until 1867, and marked silver with their name ALLAN & HAYES.
Mugs, beakers and a beer jug c.1860 are 'Marked underneath ALLAN & HAYES and a crescent tally mark'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath ALLAN & HAYES and a crescent tally mark.

facts.text: Dugald Lattey traded at 10 Government Place, Calcutta, with Arthur Pittar Lattey and Richard Thomas Callan as jewelers and diamond merchants under the firm of Allan and Hayes, later Allan and Hayes (Limited); his insolvency petition was gazetted in 1867.
facts.quote: in co-partnership with Arthur Pittar Lattey and Richard Thomas Callan, as Jewellers and Diamond Merchants, under the firm or style of Allan and Hayes

facts.text: Allan & Hayes were the successors to Lattey Brothers & Co.; Richard Thomas Callan, trading as Callan & Co., succeeded Allan & Hayes.

rows.plain: C N and Co (Charles, Nephew and Company)
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Charles, Nephew & Co., Old Court House Street, Calcutta, and Simla
rows.device: letters CN&Co (catalogued by Chiswick as CN&S)
rows.punch_set: CN&Co + lion passant + capital A (+ a letter S) + tally mark

maker.name: Charles, Nephew & Co.
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata) (9 Old Court House St); Simla 1866-1870

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Founded 1848 as successors to Pittar & Co.; Simla branch 1866; both branches closed 1870. Dated items 1864 and 1865.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta (or Simla), 1848-1870.
rows.cautions: Mark reading disputed: Chiswick consistently reads 'CN&S'; 925-1000.com's photograph shows 'CN & Co'. The A is shared with Hamilton & Co. and Pittar & Co.

facts.text: Charles, Nephew & Co. of Calcutta (1848-1870) marked their initials with a lion passant and a capital A.
Mugs, a cigar case dated 1865 and fish slices are catalogued 'Marked ... CN&S, Lion passant, and a capital A and a tally mark'; one adds an S.
facts.quote: Marked underneath CN&S, Lion passant, and a capital A and a tally mark.

facts.text: Charles, Nephew & Co., 9 Old Court House St, Calcutta 1848-1870, Simla 1866-1870: Charles John Pittar, Parke Pittar Jr. and Thomas Powell; retailing silversmiths, jewelers and watchmakers; successors to Pittar & Co.
facts.quote: Charles John Pittar, Parke Pittar Jr. and Thomas Powell. Retailing silversmiths, jewelers and watchmakers.

facts.text: Established 1848 by Charles John Pittar, his nephew Parke Pittar II, and Thomas Powell (left 1853); closed both branches in 1870.

rows.meaning: Name mark of Cooke & Kelvey, jewelers, gold and silver art workers, Old Court House Street, Calcutta
rows.device: lion's head (cabossed, i.e. face-on) as a separate punch
rows.punch_set: COOKE & KELVEY / CALCUTTA (or C&K) + a lion's head

maker.name: Cooke & Kelvey
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata), 20 Old Court House Street; branches Simla, Lahore, London; now Delhi

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Dated examples 1876 and 1877; beakers c.1860 with C&K and lion head. Founding year given variously as 1857 (925-1000.com), 1858 (forum, L&T) and 1859 (Cyclopedia of India).
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta, second half of the 19th century. The firm was a major retailer as well as maker, so the mark may be on work it bought in (it retailed Kashmir silver).
rows.cautions: A lion's head can be mistaken for a British or Continental mark. Cooke & Kelvey also retailed silver made elsewhere in India and in England.

facts.text: Cooke & Kelvey, Old Court House Street, Calcutta (founded 1858/59), marked silver COOKE & KELVEY (with CALCUTTA) or C&K.

A twin-handled cup dated 1876 is 'Marked to the foot rim edge COOKE & KELVEY CALCUTTA and lion head mark'; a christening mug c.1880 'COOKE & KELVEY, CALCUTTA and a lion's head cabossed'; a beaker c.1860 'C&K and lion head'.
facts.quote: Marked to the foot rim edge COOKE & KELVEY CALCUTTA and lion head mark.

facts.text: 925-1000.com illustrates a two-word stamp COOKE & KELVEY and a CK monogram set.

Robert Thomas Cooke, an assistant at Hamilton & Co. from 1853, opened in 1858 and in 1859 joined Charles Kelvey (from Charles, Nephew & Co. since 1855); they worked together until 1881 and the firm continued.
facts.quote: In 1859 he joins with Charles Kelvey who since 1855 had worked with Charles Nephew & Co.

facts.text: Cooke & Kelvey, Pearl and Diamond Merchants, Jewelers, Gold and Silver Art Workers, were established in 1859 and were appointed jewelers to the Earl of Mayo and every succeeding Viceroy.
facts.quote: Messrs. Cooke & Kelvey, Pearl and Diamond Merchants, Jewellers, Gold and Silver Art Workers, were established in 1859

facts.text: In Khemka family hands since 1946; partners c.1900 J. E. Calthrup and William Hill; branches London and Simla; active in Delhi.
A Kashmir bowl c.1880 was retailed by Cooke and Kelvey of Calcutta.

rows.meaning: Later initials mark of Cooke & Kelvey, Calcutta, with a word for silver and (mid-20th century) a cobra
rows.punch_set: C&K + SILVER, STERLING SILVER or SIL; c.1960 C&K + cobra + SIL

maker.name: Cooke & Kelvey
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata), 20 Old Court House Street; branches Simla, Lahore, London; now Delhi

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Undated in the sources except a cobra-marked box catalogued c.1960; the forum groups C & K - SILVER and C & K - STERLING SILVER marks.
rows.what_it_tells: 20th-century Cooke & Kelvey work or stock, Calcutta (later Delhi).
rows.cautions: The cobra mark is post-1947 by the catalogue date. 'STERLING' is a claim by the firm, not an assay.

facts.text: In the 20th century Cooke & Kelvey marked silver C&K with a word for silver.
A cigarette box c.1960 is 'Marked to interior of hinged lid with C&K, Cobra and SIL.'
facts.quote: Marked to interior of hinged lid with C&K, Cobra and SIL.

facts.text: The forum illustrates Cooke & Kelvey marks under the headings 'C & K - SILVER' and 'C & K - STERLING SILVER'.

rows.plain: C and K (Cooke and Kelvey) on Birmingham-assayed silver
rows.meaning: Cooke & Kelvey as sponsor of silver assayed at Birmingham
rows.punch_set: C & K + full Birmingham hallmarks (anchor, lion passant, date letter)

maker.name: Cooke & Kelvey
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata), 20 Old Court House Street; branches Simla, Lahore, London; now Delhi

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: One example: a novelty paper knife, Birmingham 1930, registered design 24 June 1931.
rows.what_it_tells: English-made (Birmingham) silver sold by the Calcutta firm.
rows.cautions: The item is British-made: identify it from the Birmingham hallmarks, not as Indian silver.

facts.text: A sterling silver novelty paper knife, Birmingham 1930, by Cooke and Kelvey (reg. 24th June 1931) is 'Full marked to the reverse, maker's mark C & K.'
facts.quote: Full marked to the reverse, maker's mark C & K.

rows.plain: J B and Co (J. Boseck and Company)
rows.meaning: Maker's/retailer's mark of J. Boseck & Co., jewelers, 7 Wellesley Place, Calcutta and Darjeeling
rows.punch_set: JB&Co + elephant + SIL/VER (split over two lines), or JB&Co + SILVER
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Dated items 1890 and 1907; founder John Boseck exhibited at the Calcutta International Exhibition 1883-84 and died 24 January 1899; mark registered at Birmingham Assay Office December 1909; the firm was still trading in 1953.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta (or Darjeeling) retailer-maker, c.1880-1950s. After 1909 Boseck could also sponsor Birmingham-assayed (English-made) silver.
rows.cautions: The elephant resembles Hamilton & Co.'s; check the initials. Chiswick names the founder 'Jan Boseck', the forum 'John Boseck'.

facts.text: J. Boseck & Co., jewelers of Calcutta, marked JB&Co (with SILVER or SIL VER, sometimes an elephant) and registered a mark at Birmingham in December 1909.
A pap boat c.1880 is 'Marked underneath with JB&Co, elephant and SIL over VER'; a trophy dated 1907 'Marked to the foot JB&Co and SILVER.'
facts.quote: Marked underneath with JB&Co, elephant and SIL over VER.

facts.text: J. Boseck & Co., 7 Wellesley Place, Calcutta and Darjeeling; founder John Boseck died in Calcutta 24 January 1899; registered their mark at the Birmingham Assay Office in December 1909; Arathoon Stephen (later of A. Stephen & Co.) was a former employee.
facts.quote: J. Boseck & Co. registered their mark at the Birmingham Assay Office in December 1909.

rows.meaning: Retail branch of Garrard & Co. Ltd (the London Crown Jewellers) in Dalhousie Square, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: English hallmarks of the actual maker (e.g. James Dixon & Sons, Sheffield 1909) with Garrard's Calcutta retail mark (exact wording not recorded in sources read)

maker.name: Garrard & Co. Ltd, Calcutta branch
maker.place: Calcutta (Kolkata), Dalhousie Square; also Simla and later Delhi

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Calcutta branch opened 1911; Simla before 1914.
rows.what_it_tells: English-made silver sold through Garrard's Calcutta shop.
rows.cautions: The item is English-made; date it from its British hallmarks.

facts.text: Garrard & Co. opened a Calcutta branch on Dalhousie Square in 1911.
A tea caddy by James Dixon & Sons, Sheffield 1909, was 'RETAILED BY GARRARDS, CALCUTTA'; Garrards opened their Calcutta branch on Dalhousie Square in 1911.
facts.quote: Garrards opened their Calcutta branch on Dalhousie Square in 1911

facts.text: Garrard's opened their Calcutta branch on Dalhousie Square in 1911, a Simla branch before 1914 and later Delhi.

rows.meaning: London-registered sponsor's mark of Lawrence & Mayo, opticians and instrument makers, London, Calcutta, Madras and Bombay
rows.device: letters L&M within two conjoined circles; or LM incuse
rows.punch_set: L&M (two conjoined circles) or LM incuse with London hallmarks

maker.name: Lawrence & Mayo
maker.place: London; Calcutta (from 1877, 16 Old Court House St); Madras; Bombay (Forbes St / Rampart Row)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: London Assay Office entries 15 Oct 1901 (L&M in conjoined circles), 20 Aug 1906 (LM incuse), 12 Apr 1907 (L&M in conjoined circles).
rows.what_it_tells: British-assayed silver sponsored by a firm trading in India; probably made or finished in Britain.
rows.cautions: English hallmarked; not Indian-made silver.

facts.text: Lawrence & Mayo entered marks at the London Assay Office: 'L&M' in two conjoined circles (15 Oct 1901 and 12 Apr 1907) and 'LM' incuse (20 Aug 1906); their first Indian showroom opened in Calcutta in 1877.
facts.quote: On the 15th October 1901, they entered a punch 'L&M' contained within two conjoined circles

rows.meaning: Mark of Arlington & Co., 'The Calcutta Plated Ware and Cutlery Depot', Tank Square then 3 Dalhousie Square, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: ARLINGTON & Co / CALCUTTA (two lines)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Firm 1855-c.1959 (3 Tank Square, then 3 Dalhousie Square from 1867).
rows.what_it_tells: A Calcutta dealer in plated ware and cutlery; goods were mostly imported.
rows.cautions: Usually on electroplate or imported cutlery: do not assume solid silver or Indian manufacture.

facts.text: Arlington & Co., 'The Calcutta Plated Ware and Cutlery Depot', the business of Edward Lindstedt, Samuel Harradan and Charles Vaughan, was established in 1855 at 3 Tank Square, moved to 3 Dalhousie Square in 1867 and is thought to have traded until 1959; a mark is captioned 'ARLINGTON & Co/CALCUTTA'.

rows.meaning: Chester-registered sponsor's mark of Okell & Owen, East India merchants of Liverpool and Bombay (Owen & Okell in Bombay)
rows.device: letters OO in an oval with pointed top and bottom
rows.punch_set: OO with Chester hallmarks
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Mark entered at Chester Assay Office 18 October 1899; firm established 1867.
rows.what_it_tells: British-assayed silver for a Liverpool-Bombay merchant house.
rows.cautions: Chester hallmarked; English-made.

facts.text: Okell & Owen (George Okell, George McLaren, Richard Robert Owen), established 1867, styled Owen & Okell in Bombay, entered 'OO' in an oval punch with pointed top and bottom at the Chester Assay Office on 18 October 1899.
facts.quote: On the 18th October 1899 they entered their mark 'OO' contained within an oval punch with a pointed top and bottom, with the Chester Assay Office.

rows.plain: J A (Jewanji Ardeshir; Ardeshir and Byramji)
rows.meaning: London-registered sponsor's mark of Ardeshir & Byramji, importers of Indian art, 10 Hummum Road, Bombay and 22 Oxford Street, London
rows.device: letters JA in a heart-shaped punch
rows.punch_set: JA (heart-shaped punch) with London hallmarks (import or sponsor)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Mark entered at London 11 December 1893; business c.1890-1909.
rows.what_it_tells: Indian silver imported to London by a Bombay Parsi firm would carry London marks with JA.
rows.cautions: London marks with JA do not tell you where the item was made; it may be Indian work assayed in London or British-made stock.

facts.text: Ardeshir & Byramji (Jewanji Ardeshir and Cursetji Byramji), 10 Hummum Road, Bombay and 22 Oxford Street, London, c.1890-1909 (Ardeshir & Co. from 1905), entered 'JA' in a heart-shaped punch at the London Assay Office on 11 December 1893; exhibitors at Chicago 1893.
facts.quote: They entered their mark 'JA' contained within a heart shaped punch, with the London Assay Office, on the 11th December 1893.

rows.plain: F P over B (F. P. Bhumgara and Company)
rows.meaning: London-registered sponsor's mark of F. P. Bhumgara & Co., Parsi exporters of swami silver (Madras, Bombay, London, New York)
rows.device: letters F.P above B in a heraldic shield
rows.punch_set: F.P over B (shield) with London hallmarks

maker.name: F. P. Bhumgara & Co.
maker.place: Madras (5 Mount Road); Bombay (Kalbadevi Road); London; New York

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Mark entered at London 29 September 1891.
rows.what_it_tells: Indian (mostly Madras swami) silver sent to London to be sold.
rows.cautions: London marks on Indian-made silver. Cross-reference: madras_south topic covers the Madras makers.

facts.text: F.P. Bhumgara & Co., exporters of Swami silverware, with offices in Madras, Bombay (Kalbadevi Road), London and New York, entered F.P above B in a heraldic shield at the London Assay Office on 29 September 1891.
facts.quote: F.P. Bhumgara & Co. entered their mark F.P above B contained within an heraldic shield, with the London Assay Office on the 29th September 1891.

rows.meaning: Name mark of Grish Chunder Dutt, silversmith of Bhowanipore, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Name stamp alone, usually under the base (no pseudo-hallmarks)

maker.name: Grish Chunder Dutt (later Grish Chunder Dutt & Sons)

rows.technique: stamped (incuse letters), sometimes a separate signature
rows.date_note: Active 1872-1947 per Lyon & Turnbull and Chiswick; dated items 1887, 1888, 1889, 1894. The shorter 'GRISH C DUTT, CALCUTTA' / 'GRISH. C. DUTT, CALCUTTA' appears on items of the 1880s.
rows.what_it_tells: Made by an Indian workshop in Bhowanipore, south Calcutta, typically in 'village' (rural Bengal), bamboo, river or dragon patterns. The leading Bhowanipore name.
rows.cautions: Many Calcutta village-pattern items are unmarked; the style was imitated across India (Watt 1903), so style alone does not prove a Dutt workshop. Several unrelated 'Dutt' workshops marked silver in Bhowanipore.

facts.text: Grish Chunder Dutt of Bhowanipore stamped his name under his silver as GRISH CHUNDER DUTT, BHOWANIPORE, CALCUTTA (or shorter forms).

Items are 'Marked underneath GRISH CHUNDER DUTT BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA'; bowls dated 1887 'Marked underneath GRISH C DUTT, CALCUTTA'; presentation beakers of the 1880s 'Stamped underneath GRISH. C. DUTT, CALCUTTA'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath GRISH CHUNDER DUTT BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA.

facts.text: A four-piece tea set c.1890 is 'stamped on bases GRISH CHUNDER DUTT, BHOWANIPORE, CALCUTTA'.
facts.quote: stamped on bases GRISH CHUNDER DUTT, BHOWANIPORE, CALCUTTA.

facts.text: Lyon & Turnbull catalogue a bowl marked 'GRISH, CHUNDER & DUTT, BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA' and date the maker 1872-1947, noting a gold medal at the Calcutta Industrial Exhibition 1906 and the highest award at the C.P. & Berar Exhibition, Nagpur, 1908.
facts.quote: Grish Chunder Dutt (1872 -1947) Based in Bhowanipore, in Calcutta.

facts.text: Woolley & Wallis catalogue a bowl by 'Grish, Chunder Dutt, of Bhowanipore, Calcutta, circa 1900'.
Bhowanipore, a suburb of Calcutta, was noted for its silver plate in a rural-scene style already imitated in nearly every Indian silver center by 1903.
facts.quote: CALCUTTA (Bhowanipore) produces a form of ornamentation in which rural (as distinct from hunting and jungle) scenery is depicted on a frosted surface.

rows.mark_text: GRISH CHUNDER DUTT & SONS, BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA
rows.plain: Grish Chunder Dutt and Sons, Bhowanipore, Calcutta
rows.meaning: Later firm name of the Grish Chunder Dutt workshop, Bhowanipore, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Name stamp alone

maker.name: Grish Chunder Dutt (later Grish Chunder Dutt & Sons)

rows.technique: stamped (incuse letters)
rows.date_note: Catalogued c.1900-1910; the '& SONS' form presumably later than the plain name (inference, not stated).
rows.what_it_tells: Bhowanipore workshop, early 20th century.
rows.cautions: Single auction-house source for this wording.

facts.text: A cigarette box c.1910 is 'Marked underneath GRISH CHUNDER DUTT & SONS, BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA'; a large footed bowl c.1900 is marked the same on the footrim.
facts.quote: Marked underneath GRISH CHUNDER DUTT & SONS, BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA.

forms: GRISH CHUNDER DUTT & SONS, BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA

rows.meaning: Name mark of Dass & Dutt, silversmiths, Bhowanipore, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Name stamp alone; also engraved as a signature
rows.technique: stamped (incuse letters) or engraved signature
rows.date_note: Catalogued c.1885-1920; a cup engraved 14 Sep 1909.
rows.what_it_tells: Indian workshop in Bhowanipore making village-pattern silver for British and Indian buyers.
rows.cautions: Spellings on the mark vary (Bhowanipore, Bhovanipore, Bovanipore). One Monohar Dutt bowl has 'Dass &' struck through, showing a smith moving between shops.

facts.text: Dass & Dutt of Bhowanipore stamped DASS & DUTT with BHOWANIPORE (and usually CALCUTTA).
Items are 'stamped underneath DASS&DUTT BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA' or 'Marked underneath DASS & DUTT, BHOWANIPORE'; a card case is 'signed Dass & Dutt, Bhowanipore, Calcutta'.
facts.quote: Each stamped underneath DASS&DUTT BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA.

facts.text: A collector records pepper pots c.1890 marked 'Dass & Dutt-Bhovanipore' and a bowl marked 'Dass & Dutt-Bovanipore-Calcutta'.
facts.quote: The hallmark on the bottom of each piece reads “Dass & Dutt-Bhovanipore.”

facts.text: The Dass and Dutt families were among the most prominent names of the Bhowanipore silver trade.

rows.meaning: Name mark of Goopee Nath Dutt, silversmith, Bhowanipore, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Name stamp alone; one teapot also with '830' and a second (export) mark
rows.technique: stamped (incuse letters)
rows.date_note: Dated items 1891 (Chiswick) and 1897 (L&T, presentation inscription).
rows.what_it_tells: Bhowanipore village-pattern silver of the 1890s.
rows.cautions: The '830' reading and the claim that 830 was the usual Calcutta standard come only from a collector's blog.

facts.text: Goopee Nath Dutt of Bhowanipore, Calcutta, marked silver in the 1890s (dated items 1891 and 1897).
A beaker dated 1891 and a bowl c.1900 are 'Marked underneath GOOPEE NATH DUTT BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath GOOPEE NATH DUTT BHOWANIPORE CALCUTTA.

facts.text: A presentation beaker inscribed 1897 is catalogued 'GOOPEE NATH DUTT, BHOWANIPORE, CALCUTTA, 19TH CENTURY'.
A collector's dragon-handled teapot signed Goopee Nath Dutt is marked 830 and doubly marked, one mark said to be used only for export items.
facts.quote: is marked “830,” which is the usual purity of Calcutta silver.

rows.meaning: Name mark of Monohar (Manohar) Dutt, silversmith, Bhowanipore, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Name stamp alone (one example with 'Dass &' of a Dass & Dutt stamp struck through)
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Catalogued c.1890-1900.
rows.what_it_tells: Bhowanipore workshop that apparently left Dass & Dutt.
rows.cautions: Mark wording recorded only by a collector's blog (case as transcribed there); Chiswick spells the name Monohur.

facts.text: A Bhowanipore silversmith named Monohar (Monohur) Dutt marked bowls c.1890-1900.
Two bowls c.1890 are marked 'Monohar Dutt, Bhowanipore, Calcutta', the second also with 'Dass &' struck through, suggesting the smith left the Dass & Dutt shop.
facts.quote: Bowl 2 marked: Monohar Dutt, Dass & [sic strikethrough] Dutt, Bhowanipore, Calcutta

facts.text: Chiswick sold a pair of Bhowanipore village-pattern bowls c.1900 'by Monohur Dutt'.

rows.plain: S D and Co (unidentified Calcutta retailer)
rows.meaning: Unidentified mark on Calcutta village-pattern silver, with STERLING SILVER
rows.punch_set: SD&CO + STERLING SILVER
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: One cup dated 1902.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta-style work of c.1902 sold or made by an unidentified 'SD & Co.'
rows.cautions: Attribution open: Chiswick suggests, tentatively, Sri Ram Janki Das (a Delhi jeweler at the 1902-03 Delhi Exhibition).

facts.text: A Calcutta cup dated 1902 is 'Marked underneath SD&CO, STERLING SILVER'; the cataloguer suggests a possible link with Sri Ram Janki Das.
facts.quote: Marked underneath SD&CO, STERLING SILVER.

rows.meaning: Unidentified initials on Calcutta club silver, with STERLING SILVER
rows.punch_set: STERLING SILVER + K.P.D.
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: One Bengal Club mustard or chutney pot catalogued c.1930.
rows.what_it_tells: Calcutta-retailed club silver of the 1930s.
rows.cautions: Maker unidentified.

facts.text: A 'Bengal club' mustard or chutney pot, Calcutta c.1930, is 'Marked underneath STERLING SILVER K.P.D.'
facts.quote: Marked underneath STERLING SILVER K.P.D.

rows.meaning: Unidentified maker's initials on early Calcutta silver
rows.punch_set: KD + tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: One pap boat catalogued Calcutta c.1830.
rows.what_it_tells: Possibly an early-19th-century Calcutta maker.
rows.cautions: Unidentified; single catalogue attribution.

facts.text: A pap boat 'Calcutta circa 1830 by KD' is 'Marked with KD and tally mark.'
facts.quote: Marked with KD and tally mark.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Mathies & Barron, jewelers, silversmiths and watchmakers, 7 Forbes Street and later Rampart Row, Bombay
rows.device: letters M & B in a rectangular punch
rows.punch_set: Urn + M & B + lower-case f (one recorded set)

maker.name: Mathies & Barron (Thomas Mathie(s) and James Barron)
maker.place: Bombay (Mumbai), 7 Forbes Street, later Rampart Row

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Partnership July 1828 until Thomas Mathie's death in 1838.
rows.what_it_tells: Bombay, 1828-1838: the main early European silversmiths of Bombay, much rarer than Calcutta or Madras work.
rows.cautions: The urn resembles Hamilton & Co.'s urn punch (Calcutta). Spelled Mathie or Mathies in sources.

facts.text: Mathies & Barron were jewelers and watchmakers in Bombay; Thomas Mathies died in 1838.
A mug's base bears 'an urn, the maker's mark of an upper case M & B in a rectangular punch, and a lower case f', consistent with Mathies & Barron of Bombay.
facts.quote: Three marks: an urn, the maker’s mark of an upper case ‘M & B’ in a rectangular punch, and a lower case ‘f’ appear near the centre of the base.

facts.text: Thomas Mathie (1802-38) and James Barron (1806-52), a London-trained watchmaker, formed a partnership in July 1828 at 7 Forbes Street, later Rampart Row, Bombay, ending with Mathie's death in 1838 (Wilkinson 1987, pp.15, 130-131).
facts.quote: Thomas subsequently formed a partnership in July 1828 with James Barron (1806-52)

facts.text: The Asiatic Journal (1838) records the death on 8 Sept. of Mr Thomas Mathies of the firm of Mathies and Barron, Jewelers and Watchmakers, aged 38.
facts.quote: In the Fort, Mr. Thomas Mathies, of the firm of Mathies and Barron, Jewellers and Watchmakers. Aged 38.

facts.text: Sotheby's sold a brandy warmer 'Mathies & Barron, Bombay, circa 1830', marked on base, illustrated in Wilkinson 1987 p.130; Woolley & Wallis a waiter 'by Thomas Mathies and James Barron, Bombay circa 1830'.
In Bombay, Mathies & Barron were a key firm.
facts.quote: In Bombay, Mathies & Barron were a key firm.

rows.plain: G R and Co (George Regel and Company)
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of George Regel & Co., Medows Street, Bombay
rows.punch_set: GR&Co + an X mark + tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Active 1844-52 per Chiswick (after Wilkinson 1987).
rows.what_it_tells: Bombay, mid-19th century; very rare.
rows.cautions: Single auction house (two Chiswick texts). GR is also a British royal cipher; here it is a firm's initials.

facts.text: A set of four cruets, Bombay c.1850, are 'Each marked to the foot GR&Co, and with an X mark as well as a tally mark'; the firm worked from Medow's Street and is described in the Bombay Directory as jeweler, sculptor, undertaker and watchmaker (Wilkinson 1987). [directory description is Wilkinson 1987 as cited by Chiswick]
facts.quote: Each marked to the foot GR&Co, and with an X mark as well as a tally mark.

facts.text: Chiswick's survey article illustrates the same cruets as 'Bombay circa 1850 by George Regel and Co (active 1844-52)'.

rows.meaning: Initials of Tarachand Pursram Ramswami, jewelers, diamond merchants and silversmiths, 63 Meadow Street, Bombay (branches Calcutta and Rangoon)
rows.punch_set: T.P.R + T 90S (engraved)

maker.name: Tarachand Pursram Ramswami
maker.place: Bombay (Mumbai), 63 Meadow Street; branches Calcutta and Rangoon

rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Exhibited at Delhi 1902-03; items catalogued c.1900-1920.
rows.what_it_tells: Bombay dealer-retailer; it sold swami-pattern silver, some of it made in Bangalore, so the maker may be elsewhere in India.
rows.cautions: Retailer, not necessarily maker: Chiswick attributes some T.P.R-retailed items to Bangalore (probably C. Krishniah Chetty). Many of its items are unmarked.

facts.text: Tarachand Pursram (Ramswami) of Meadow Street, Bombay, were jewelers and silversmiths c.1902.
A Bombay tea service c.1910 in Madras swami pattern is 'Each engraved underneath T.P.R, T 90S.'
facts.quote: Each engraved underneath T.P.R, T 90S.

facts.text: Tarachand Pursram Ramswami, 63 Meadow Street, Bombay, exhibited old and new jewelry and Indian art wares at Delhi 1902-03 and had branches in Calcutta and Rangoon; jewelers, diamond merchants and silversmiths.
facts.quote: The firm have branches in Calcutta and Rangoon and conduct an extensive business as dealers in art curios as well as being jewellers, diamond merchants, and silver-smiths.

facts.text: A Bombay consular list of 1902 names 'Tarachund Pursram, Meadows street' among Bombay jewelers and silversmiths.
Chiswick catalogues Bangalore items c.1900-1910 'retailed by Tarachand Pursram Ramswam of Bombay', one 'probably by Cotha Krishniah Chetty'.

rows.plain: F N C O (unidentified Bombay maker)
rows.meaning: Unidentified (presumed maker's) mark on Bombay silver, with T 90 in a spade-shaped punch and sometimes BOMBAY
rows.device: letters F N C O in a shaped punch
rows.punch_set: T 90 (spade-shaped punch) + F N C O (+ BOMBAY)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Catalogued c.1920.
rows.what_it_tells: Bombay work of the early 20th century.
rows.cautions: Maker unidentified; reading 'F N C O' is the cataloguer's.

facts.text: Three bowls, Bombay c.1920, are 'Each marked underneath with T 90 in a spade shaped punch, and a maker's mark (presumably) F N C O in a shaped punch'; the same marks with the additional stamp BOMBAY were noted on a hunting-pattern cup and cover.
facts.quote: Each marked underneath with T 90 in a spade shaped punch, and a maker’s mark (presumably) F N C O in a shaped punch.

rows.plain: T 90 / T 95 (number mark on western Indian silver)
rows.meaning: Number mark of the form T90, T 90, T95 or T 90S on early-20th-century silver from Bombay, Poona, Karachi (and Lucknow); generally taken as a statement of silver content, but no source read explains it
rows.device: letter T with a number, sometimes in a spade-shaped punch
rows.punch_set: Struck with a maker's name or initials (J. MANIKRAI / SOOSANIA + T95 + KARACHI; LM over T90; F N C O + T 90 + BOMBAY; T.P.R + T 90S)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: All examples catalogued c.1900-1930 (one Bombay/Poona mug dated 1908).
rows.fineness: Not stated by sources; probably a claimed silver content of 90 or 95 per cent (unverified)
rows.what_it_tells: Points to 20th-century western Indian (Bombay/Karachi/Poona) or Lucknow silver.
rows.cautions: Meaning unverified: it is widely read as 'touch 90/95' (parts silver per 100), but none of the sources consulted state this; do not quote a fineness from it without a test. Cross-reference: kutch_north and dating topics.

facts.text: Marks of the form T90 / T95 occur on early-20th-century silver from Bombay, Karachi and Lucknow.

Karachi items are 'Marked underneath J. MANIKRAI, T95, KARACHI' and 'SOOSANIA, T95, KARACHI'; others 'LM and T90'; a Bombay or Poona christening mug dated 1908 'Marked underneath T90'; Bombay bowls 'T 90 in a spade shaped punch'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath J. MANIKRAI, T95, KARACHI.

facts.text: A Lucknow bowl is catalogued 'STAMPED T.90'.
facts.quote: STAMPED T.90, LION BELOW MOUNTAINS SIGNATURE

rows.meaning: Name mark of Narotamdas Bhau (Jhaveri), jewelers, Sheikh Memon Street and later 437 Lamington Road, Bombay
rows.punch_set: Narotamdas Bhau / Bombay / Silver (three lines)

maker.name: Narotamdas Bhau (now N. Bhau (Jewellers) Pvt. Ltd.)

rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Firm founded 1864; advertisements 1918-1958.
rows.what_it_tells: Bombay jeweler-silversmith; still trading.
rows.cautions: Single forum source for the silver mark wording.

facts.text: Narotamdas Bhau Jhaveri, Bhau Mansion, Sheikh Memon Street, later 437 Lamington Road, Bombay, founded 1864, used the trade mark 'N.B.J.'; silverware noted marked 'Narotamdas Bhau/Bombay/Silver'.
facts.quote: Silverware noted as being marked 'Narotamdas Bhau/Bombay/Silver'.

rows.meaning: Untraced maker's initials on Karachi silver, struck with T90
rows.punch_set: LM over T90
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Catalogued c.1920.
rows.what_it_tells: Karachi, early 20th century.
rows.cautions: Maker untraced; not to be confused with Lawrence & Mayo's London-registered LM.

facts.text: A Karachi teapot c.1920 is 'Marked underneath with LM and T90' and a belt 'LM over T90'; catalogued as untraced.
facts.quote: Marked underneath with LM and T90.

rows.mark_text: JARADI MOHANLAL. VASRAM. JUNAGHADH VALA. MADE IN KARACHI CAMP.
rows.plain: Jaradi Mohanlal Vasram, Junagadh-wala, made in Karachi Camp
rows.meaning: Maker's stamp of Jaradi Mohanlal Vasram, 'of Junagadh', working in Karachi Camp
rows.punch_set: Full stamp alone
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: One casket catalogued c.1920 (with a view of the Imperial Bank of India, Karachi).
rows.what_it_tells: Karachi work by a smith from Junagadh in Kathiawar.
rows.cautions: Single example. 'VALA' (-vala/-wala) means 'of' or 'from' Junagadh.

facts.text: A Karachi casket c.1920 is 'Stamped underneath JARADI MOHANLAL. VASRAM. JUNAGHADH VALA. MADE IN KARACHI CAMP.'
facts.quote: Stamped underneath JARADI MOHANLAL. VASRAM. JUNAGHADH VALA. MADE IN KARACHI CAMP.

forms: JARADI MOHANLAL. VASRAM. JUNAGHADH VALA. MADE IN KARACHI CAMP.
