JARADI MOHANLAL. VASRAM. JUNAGHADH VALA. MADE IN KARACHI CAMP

rows.meaning: Applied maker's boss (plaque) of Heerappa Boochena, goldsmith and silversmith of Poona
rows.device: applied maker's boss (exact wording not recorded in sources read)
rows.punch_set: Applied boss on some items; most work unmarked
rows.technique: applied (soldered) boss
rows.date_note: A cup dated 1883 bears his applied boss (Dreweatts 2021, as cited by Chiswick); exhibited at Delhi 1902-03.
rows.what_it_tells: Poona's leading silversmith; finely embossed figural scenes in arcades combined with Kutch-type work.
rows.cautions: Most Poona silver is unmarked and attributed by style. Poona work mixes Madras, Kutch, Lucknow and Burmese motifs and is easily misattributed.

facts.text: Heerappa Boochena (Hitapa Buchana) was a goldsmith-silversmith of Poona working c.1883-1903.
A Poona silver tray with hunting figures (Rs. 528) and a silver bowl (Rs. 440) were shown by Hitapa Buchana, goldsmith of Poona, at the Delhi Exhibition 1902-03.
facts.quote: a silver tray [tahdk) with hunting figures, made by Hitapa Buchana, goldsmith of Poona, Rs. 528

facts.text: Heerappa Boochena, believed to have come from or trained in Lucknow, was the main craftsman in Poona; a dated presentation cup of 1883 bears his applied maker's boss.
facts.quote: this piece bears his applied maker’s boss

rows.meaning: Elephant punch used as a house or 'town' mark by Hamilton & Co., Calcutta (from 1808 to the 1970s), and also by J. Boseck & Co.
rows.device: elephant, standing, in a rectangular or shaped punch
rows.punch_set: With H&Co (+ A, urn, thistle, tally; later SILVER or a date letter) or with JB&Co + SIL/VER
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Hamilton & Co. stated in 1919 that its mark had been H. & Co. with an elephant for over a hundred years; used until the firm closed (1970-73).
rows.what_it_tells: An elephant beside firm initials on English-style silver points to Calcutta, almost always Hamilton & Co.
rows.cautions: Long mistaken for an Inverness (Scotland) town mark; Jackson's 1921 list still placed a Hamilton item under Inverness. Not a British assay mark. J. Boseck & Co. also used an elephant.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co.'s elephant punch was taken for an Inverness (Scottish) town mark.
Hamilton's elephant punch was mistaken for an Inverness town mark in early publications.
facts.quote: In early publications they are often seen in the Inverness section as the elephant punch was mistaken for an Inverness town mark.

facts.text: Jackson (1921) lists a 'Hamilton & Co.' strainer among Inverness marks with a footnote to compare the Calcutta marks on p.473, where he records the firm's 1919 statement that its mark had long been H. & Co. with an elephant.
facts.quote: Compare with Calcutta marks, p. 473, supra.

facts.text: J. Boseck & Co. marked a pap boat c.1880 with JB&Co, an elephant and SIL over VER.

rows.meaning: Imitation of the English sterling lion passant, struck by Calcutta firms with their initials and a letter A or B
rows.device: lion walking to the left, one forepaw raised, in a shaped or rectangular punch; crowned on Twentyman, Beck & Co. items
rows.punch_set: C&Co + lion + B (Cropley); TB&Co + crowned lion + lion rampant (Twentyman, Beck); T&Co + lion (Twentyman & Co.); P&Co + lion + A (Pittar); APL&Co + lion + B (Pittar, Lattey); LB&Co + lion + B, or with anchor, gothic letter and crown (Lattey Bros); CN&Co + lion + A (Charles, Nephew)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Recorded on Calcutta silver from Cropley & Co. (1819) to Charles, Nephew & Co. (to 1870).
rows.what_it_tells: With Indian-firm initials and no town mark or cyclic date letter, it points to Calcutta, c.1819-1870. It guarantees nothing about fineness.
rows.cautions: Easily read as English sterling. A genuine British set includes a town mark and a cyclic date letter; the Calcutta sets have firm initials, a constant A or B (or other device) and often a tally mark instead.

facts.text: Calcutta firms struck an imitation lion passant beside their initials.
Cropley's caster is punched with a simulated sterling mark, the lion passant, a practice illegal in England.
facts.quote: This caster is also punched with a simulated sterling mark, the lion passant, a practice illegal in England.

facts.text: Chiswick describes Pittar & Co. marks as 'P & Co, pseudo lion passant, and capital A' and Twentyman & Co. as 'T&Co, pseudo lion passant and tally mark'.
facts.quote: Marked underneath with P & Co, pseudo lion passant, and capital A.

rows.plain: Roman capital A or B (Calcutta letter mark)
rows.meaning: Single capital letter A or B struck with Calcutta firm marks; not a date letter (except Hamilton & Co. from 1937)
rows.device: Roman capital A or B in a square or shaped punch
rows.punch_set: A: Hamilton & Co. (c.1808-1914), Pittar & Co., Charles, Nephew & Co.; B: Cropley & Co., Pittar, Lattey & Co., Lattey Brothers
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: From Robert Hamilton's earliest marks (1808) to c.1914 when Hamilton replaced the A with SILVER (ASCAS); from 1937 Hamilton letters are true date letters.
rows.what_it_tells: An A or B next to Calcutta initials looks like a date letter but is a constant house letter.
rows.cautions: Do not read A or B with a British date-letter table. The V&A notes A and B were not used consistently enough to mean grades of quality.

facts.text: Calcutta firms struck a single Roman capital A or B with their initials.
'A' and 'B' marks were frequently used in Calcutta, but not consistently enough to denote levels of quality; Cropley mainly used B.
facts.quote: 'A' and 'B' marks were frequently used in Calcutta, but not consistently enough to denote levels of quality.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co.'s marks combined H&Co with an elephant and Roman capital A; from 1937 a date letter replaced the traditional Roman A.
facts.quote: From 1937 a date letter was introduced in place of the traditional Roman 'A'.

rows.plain: Lion rampant holding a crown (East India Company crest)
rows.meaning: Lion rampant holding a crown, reproducing the East India Company crest, used by Twentyman, Beck & Co., Calcutta
rows.punch_set: TB&Co + lion rampant + crowned lion passant + tally mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Recorded only with Twentyman, Beck & Co., 1821-23.
rows.what_it_tells: A strong pointer to Twentyman, Beck & Co., Calcutta, 1821-23.
rows.cautions: Not a Scottish, Dutch or Continental lion mark. Wilkinson suggests it was used like a royal warrant.

facts.text: Twentyman, Beck & Co.'s marks include a lion rampant.
Wilkinson (1973, p.155, quoted by Sotheby's): the lion rampant reproduces the crest of the East India Company and may have been used like a royal warrant. (quoted in Sotheby's 2013 catalogue)
facts.quote: The lion rampant mark is a reproduction of the crest of the East India Company

facts.text: Chiswick records TB&Co with a lion rampant and a lion passant on items of 1821-23.

rows.meaning: Anchor with rope (fouled anchor) struck by Calcutta silversmiths, notably W. H. Twentyman and Lattey Brothers
rows.punch_set: WHT + crescent and star + anchor + tally (Twentyman, 1815-21); LB(&Co) + anchor + lion passant + gothic letter + crown + tally (Lattey Brothers, c.1850)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Recorded on Twentyman (1815-21) and Lattey Brothers (c.1850) items; 925-1000.com shows an anchor with John Hunt's JH.
rows.what_it_tells: With Calcutta initials, a fouled anchor is not the Birmingham assay mark or a Greenock town mark.
rows.cautions: Twentyman's anchor led to his work being attributed to Greenock; check the initials and the rest of the set before reading any anchor as a British town mark.

facts.text: Twentyman's Calcutta marks include a fouled anchor.
Work by the 'unknown WHT' was attributed to Greenock, presumably due to the anchor mark.
facts.quote: presumably due to the use of an anchor mark on many of his pieces.

facts.text: Chiswick records 'WHT, a crescent and star, a fouled anchor' (Twentyman) and 'LB, fouled anchor, lion passant, gothic L, crown' (Lattey Brothers).
facts.quote: Marked underneath with LB, fouled anchor, lion passant, gothic L, and crown.

rows.meaning: A king's head punch struck by Hippolitus Poignand, Calcutta, imitating the British sovereign's-head duty mark
rows.punch_set: HP + king's head + tally (with a star device)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Poignand's working years.
rows.what_it_tells: On Calcutta work it is decoration of the mark set, not evidence of British duty paid.
rows.cautions: Single source for the head on Calcutta silver.

facts.text: A salver c.1800 by Hippolitus Poignand is 'Marked underneath with HP, King's head mark, and tally mark.'
facts.quote: Marked underneath with HP, King's head mark, and tally mark.

rows.plain: Uncrowned leopard's head with a year in figures (Dormieux)
rows.meaning: Imitation London leopard's head struck with a four-figure year and a thistle by Francis Dormieux & Co., Calcutta
rows.device: uncrowned leopard's (lion's) face; separate punch with year e.g. 1813, 1816
rows.punch_set: (?Indian-script mark) + thistle + year + leopard's head + F.D
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Years 1813 and 1816 recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: A year in plain figures next to an uncrowned leopard's head and F.D points to Dormieux, Calcutta.
rows.cautions: The leopard's head imitates the London town mark, and the four-figure year can be mistaken for a genuine date; neither is an assay mark.

facts.text: Dormieux struck a year in figures with a leopard's head and F.D.
V&A salver: thistle, date-mark 1816, uncrowned leopard's head, FD.
facts.quote: a leopard's head uncrowned (worn)

facts.text: 925-1000.com illustrates 1813, a leopard's head and F.D.

rows.meaning: Thistle punch (imitating the Edinburgh standard mark), sometimes with an imitation Edinburgh castle, on early Calcutta silver
rows.punch_set: Thistle with I.M (Mair, 1789-96); with F.D and a year (Dormieux, 1813-21); with H&Co, elephant, A (Hamilton, c.1821-1860); castle + thistle with M&Co. (Middleton, 1822-34)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Range of the recorded users.
rows.what_it_tells: Thistle-marked silver without an Edinburgh date letter, or with Calcutta initials, may be Calcutta work.
rows.cautions: This is why so much Calcutta silver was once filed as Scottish. ASCAS queries whether Hamilton's device is really a thistle.

facts.text: Middleton & Co.'s mug carries imitations of the castle and thistle marks of the Edinburgh Assay Office.
facts.quote: imitations of the castle and thistle marks of the Edinburgh Assay Office.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co. used a thistle(?) c.1821-c.1860.
facts.quote: The marks are what is believed to be a thistle, an urn, the initials ‘H&Co.’, an elephant and the letter ‘A’.

facts.text: Wilkinson: when he began his study most items were mistakenly attributed to Scottish origins.
facts.quote: most pieces were mistakenly attributed to Scottish origins.

rows.plain: Urn or 'cup and cover' (Hamilton & Co.; Mathies & Barron)
rows.meaning: Urn-shaped punch used by Hamilton & Co., Calcutta, on more important items c.1815-1850, and by Mathies & Barron, Bombay
rows.punch_set: H&Co + elephant + urn + A (+ thistle, tally); urn + M & B + f (Mathies & Barron)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Hamilton use c.1812/1815-1850 (ASCAS; Wilkinson 1999 via Backman).
rows.what_it_tells: On Hamilton work it suggests a better item of c.1815-1850; on a Bombay item with M & B it points to Mathies & Barron.
rows.cautions: Auction houses call the same punch 'urn' or 'cup and cover'.

facts.text: Hamilton & Co. struck an urn ('cup and cover') punch with H&Co, elephant and A in the first half of the 19th century.
The urn mark tends to appear only on more important Hamilton items and was used from 1815 to 1850 (Wilkinson 1999, p.53). (as cited by Michael Backman)
facts.quote: the urn mark tends to have only appeared on more important pieces and was used from 1815 to 1850.

facts.text: Chiswick describes Hamilton pans c.1830-1850 marked 'H&Co, an elephant, a cup and cover, Roman capital A'.
A Mathies & Barron mug bears an urn, M & B and a lower-case f.

rows.plain: Tally marks (small symbols and numbers on Calcutta silver)
rows.meaning: Small incuse symbols or numbers struck with Calcutta firm marks, thought to identify the Indian workman paid for the item
rows.device: small incuse device: lotus, crescent, trefoil, annulet, pellet, pelleted or crossed square, trident, three dots, or a number (e.g. 22)
rows.punch_set: Struck with Hamilton, Twentyman, Pittar, Lattey, Nephew, Allan & Hayes marks
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Recorded from Poignand (c.1800) to Hamilton (c.1880-90).
rows.what_it_tells: A tiny extra symbol beside the firm marks is normal on Calcutta silver and supports a Calcutta attribution.
rows.cautions: Not a date, assay or standard mark. The workman explanation is a dealer's interpretation ('seem to').

facts.text: Small 'tally marks' are struck beside the firm marks on Calcutta silver.
Tally marks are often found on colonial Calcutta silver and seem to identify the native silversmith responsible so that he would be paid for his work.
facts.quote: Tally marks often are found on colonial Calcutta silver and seem to have been used to identify the native silversmith who was responsible for producing the piece

facts.text: Catalogued tally marks include lotus, crescent, trefoil, annulet, pellet, pelleted square, crossed square and trident; Sotheby's records 'tally mark 22'.
facts.quote: marked on base with tally mark 22

rows.meaning: Star-like device struck by Hippolitus Poignand and similar to one used by Joseph Rondo, Calcutta
rows.punch_set: Star + HP + head (Poignand)
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Poignand 1793-1805; Rondo active 1805-1818 (Chiswick).
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Calcutta, c.1793-1818.
rows.cautions: Rondo's own initials punch was not found in sources read.

facts.text: Poignand's star device is similar to one used by Joseph Rondo, who bought Poignand's stock after his death.
Joseph Rondo was active 1805-1818; a gold snuff box by him dated 1811 is in a private collection.
facts.quote: dated 1811 by Jospeh Rondo (active 1805-1818)

rows.plain: SILVER / STERLING SILVER / SIL (word marks on Indian silver)
rows.meaning: Word marks struck by Calcutta and Bombay firms in the 20th century, often replacing pseudo-hallmarks
rows.punch_set: With firm initials: H&Co + elephant + SILVER (Hamilton from c.1914); JB&Co + SILVER or SIL/VER (Boseck); C&K + SIL or STERLING SILVER (Cooke & Kelvey); SD&CO + STERLING SILVER; STERLING SILVER + K.P.D.
rows.technique: struck with a punch (incuse or in a shaped punch)
rows.date_note: Hamilton struck SILVER at least from 1914 (ASCAS).
rows.fineness: Claims silver or sterling (92.5%); unverified by any assay
rows.what_it_tells: A firm's own claim that the item is silver (or sterling); Indian silver was never assayed under British law.
rows.cautions: Not an assay. Indian silver varied widely in fineness: rupee silver was below English sterling, and the London assay office broke up Indian plate in 1881 for being 7.5-15 dwt worse than standard.

facts.text: 20th-century Calcutta firms struck SILVER or STERLING SILVER with their marks.
Hamilton & Co. struck the word 'silver' at least from 1914.
facts.quote: bears the word 'silver' which was then struck at least from this date on

facts.text: Chiswick records SILVER, STERLING SILVER and SIL on Hamilton, Boseck, Cooke & Kelvey and SD&Co items; Woolley & Wallis a Calcutta bowl 'marked Sterling Silver'.
The Goldsmiths' Company (1883) said the Orr consignment of Indian plate was nowhere better than 7.5 dwt and mostly 15 dwt worse than the English standard, rupee silver being 2-2.5 dwt worse.
facts.quote: rupee silver varies from 2 to 2½ dwts. only worse than the English standard

facts.text: Indian silver was never of a single consistent standard of purity; rupees were 91.7% silver but melted coin could not always be relied on.
facts.quote: the silver of India is vastly inconsistent with regards to the purity of the silver.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Hugh Gordon, silversmith in Madras from 1793, founder of the Gordon silversmithing line of Madras
rows.device: thistle, in a separate chamfered rectangular punch
rows.punch_set: 'H G' in Roman capitals in a rectangular punch, with a thistle in a chamfered rectangular punch (as described on one mustard pot, c.1795)
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Hugh Gordon reached Madras in 1792 and opened his own business in 1793 (dealer biographies); end of his use of the mark not established.
rows.what_it_tells: An 'HG' with a thistle on Georgian-style silver may be Madras work of the 1790s rather than Scottish provincial silver.
rows.cautions: 'HG' is a very common pair of initials in British silver, and the thistle is a Scottish device (Edinburgh standard mark, and a pseudo-mark used by several Indian colonial makers). Do not attribute on the initials alone; the thistle-and-HG combination is recorded from a single Wilkinson-described example.

facts.text: Hugh Gordon, son of the Aberdeen silversmith James Gordon, moved to Madras in 1792 and opened his own business the next year.
facts.quote: originally started by Hugh Gordon, son of James Gordon, silversmith in Aberdeen

facts.text: A mustard pot of c.1795 attributed to Hugh Gordon of Madras bears 'H G' in Roman capitals in a rectangular punch with a thistle in a chamfered rectangular punch.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Gordon & Lovell, North Gate Street, Madras (George Gordon I, Francis Lovell and Robert Gordon II)
rows.punch_set: 'G&L' in a rectangular punch (photographed example); companion punches not recorded
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Partnership dates from Wilkinson 1987 as compiled by 925-1000.com.
rows.what_it_tells: Places an item in Madras in the first decade of the 19th century.
rows.cautions: Single compiled source for the mark. A 'G&L' punch is not unique to this firm; check the style (Georgian, Madras) and any pseudo-marks.

facts.text: Gordon & Lovell, of North Gate Street, Madras, worked 1803-1807; partners George Gordon I, Francis Lovell and Robert Gordon II.
A pair of Indian colonial silver tankards 'Gordon and Lovell, Madras, circa 1805', marked on the bases, was offered at Sotheby's (Edith and Stuart Cary Welch Collection).

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of James Cox, silversmith of Popham's Broadway and later the Esplanade, Madras ('I' standing for 'J')
rows.punch_set: 'IC' in script capitals in a rectangular punch (photographed example)
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Working dates from Wilkinson 1987 (via 925-1000.com); the 1839 Madras Almanac independently lists 'Cox, J.' at the Esplanade among jewelers and silversmiths.
rows.what_it_tells: An 'IC' mark on Georgian-style silver with Madras provenance may be Cox's; partnerships Johnson & Cox (1806-1812), Cox, Johnson & Monin (1822) and Cox & Monin (1823-1825) used other names.
rows.cautions: 'IC' was used by many British silversmiths (I for J was standard engraving practice). Attribution needs Madras context.

facts.text: James Cox worked in Madras 1801-1844, at Popham's Broadway and, after 1822, the Esplanade; partnerships Johnson & Cox 1806-1812, Cox, Johnson & Monin 1822, Cox & Monin 1823-1825.
The Madras Almanac for 1839 lists 'Cox, J.' at the Esplanade under 'Jewelers and Silversmiths'.
facts.quote: Jewellers and Silversmiths. ... Cox, J. - - - Esplanade

rows.meaning: Maker's mark 'GG' of George Gordon & Co., Popham's Broadway, Madras
rows.device: a thistle beside the initials in one photographed punch
rows.punch_set: 'GG' followed by a thistle (photographed example); the firm also used 'GG&Co' (see separate row)
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Firm dates; which years each Gordon punch was used is not established.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to the leading Madras silversmiths of the 1820s-1840s.
rows.cautions: 'GG' with a thistle can be mistaken for Scottish provincial silver. A different, later 'Gordon & Co.' (Wallajah Road, Triplicane) is listed among Madras jewelers in 1918 and is not the same firm.

facts.text: A punch reading 'GG' with a thistle is illustrated for George Gordon & Co., Madras.
A dealer describes a Madras tankard of c.1830 as hallmarked 'GG' for George Gordon & Co.

variants: GG&Co followed by a further letter for the 1845-1848 partnership with Peter and Alexander Orr
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of George Gordon & Co., silversmiths, jewelers, watch and clock makers, 18 Popham's Broadway, Madras
rows.punch_set: 'GG&Co' (with small raised 'o') in a rectangular punch, usually struck alone without pseudo-hallmarks ('struck with makers mark GG & CO only')
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.where_on_object: back of flatware stems; underside or near rim of hollowware
rows.date_note: Founded 1821 by George Gordon II, Robert Gordon III, John Law and Andrew Barron; Peter and Alexander Orr partners 1843/1845-1848; succeeded 1848/49 (925-1000 names Phillips & Co.; Orr-history sources say the Orrs took over).
rows.what_it_tells: A 'GG&Co' mark on Georgian/William IV-style silver indicates Madras manufacture or retail, 1821-1848.
rows.cautions: Successor disputed: 925-1000.com (from Wilkinson) says the Gordon firm was succeeded by Phillips & Co.; Wikipedia, dealer and Orr-family accounts say the Orr brothers took over George Gordon & Co. in 1849. Don't confuse with the 20th-century 'Gordon & Co.' of Wallajah Road, Triplicane. A further letter after 'GG&Co' on one photographed punch (1845-1848 period) is uncertain.

facts.text: George Gordon & Co. was in business at Madras between about 1821 and 1848.
facts.quote: George Gordon & Co. was in business at Madras between about 1821 and 1848.

facts.text: The firm was founded by George Gordon II, Robert Gordon III, John Law and Andrew Barron at 18 Popham's Broadway.
John Law is listed in 1834 as of the firm of Messrs. Gordon and Co., Madras.
The 1839 Madras Almanac lists 'Gordon, G., & Co.' at Popham's Broadway under 'Jewelers and Silversmiths, Watch and Clock Makers'.
facts.quote: Jewellers and Silversmiths, Watch and Clock Makers. Gordon, G, & Co. Popham's Broadway

facts.text: Flatware by George Gordon & Co., Madras, c.1840 was 'struck with makers mark GG & CO only'.
facts.quote: struck with makers mark 'GG & CO' only, by George Gordon & Co, Madras c.1840

facts.text: A firm employee, Andrew Barron, died in Madras on 15 July 1832.
Other auction lots of George Gordon & Co. silver (a covered jar of 1830-40; a basting spoon of c.1850) are likewise described as bearing the maker's mark only.
facts.quote: maker's mark only, by George Gordon & Co. of Madras c.1850

rows.plain: Manufactured by P. Orr and Co., Madras, 1855
rows.meaning: Engraved manufacturer's signature of P. Orr & Co., Madras (the firm's name 1854-c.1860, before P. Orr & Sons)
rows.technique: engraved
rows.where_on_object: front of the cup (V&A centrepiece), with 'ORR' stamped on the back
rows.date_note: Firm styled P. Orr & Co. from 1854 (Wilkinson via 925-1000); the V&An item is engraved and dated 1855.
rows.what_it_tells: An item signed 'P. Orr & Co.' dates from Peter Orr's own firm before his sons joined (c.1854-1860).
rows.cautions: Engraved dates record an event or exhibition, not necessarily the year of making.

facts.text: The V&A centrepiece 02616(IS) is engraved 'Manufactured by P.Orr & Co. Madras 1855' on the front of the cup and stamped 'ORR' on the back.
facts.quote: Manufactured by P.Orr & Co. Madras 1855 (engraved on front of cup) ORR (stamped on the back)

facts.text: Peter Nicholas Orr (1803-1887) set up his own shop on Mount Road c.1851; in 1854 it became P. Orr & Co.
facts.quote: Set up own shop c.1851 1854 became P. Orr & Co.

facts.text: The 1853 Madras New Almanac lists 'Orr, Peter' at Mount Road (among watch and clock repairers; OCR columns jumbled).

variants: ORR on the side of a foot with P ORR & SONS MADRAS under the base
rows.meaning: Maker's mark (stamped pseudo-hallmark) of Peter Orr / P. Orr & Co. / P. Orr & Sons, Madras
rows.punch_set: 'ORR' in capitals in a rectangular punch, often struck alone

maker.name: Peter Orr; P. Orr & Co.; P. Orr & Sons

rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.where_on_object: back of spoon bowls near the stem; back of hollowware; side of a foot rim
rows.date_note: Used by Peter Orr's own firm from c.1851 and continued by P. Orr & Sons; 925-1000.com (after Wilkinson) gives 'Mark used 1860-c.1900' for the Orr & Sons entry. V&A examples dated 1855 and c.1876. DISPUTED: one dealer says 'ORR' was used only until about 1860, but the V&A records 'ORR' on Orr & Sons spoons of c.1876.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies the leading Madras silversmith of the second half of the 19th century, the principal maker of 'swami' silver.
rows.cautions: ORR alone does not distinguish Peter Orr's early firm from P. Orr & Sons. 'ORR' is also an English/Scottish surname; British-hallmarked silver by other Orrs exists. Many unmarked swami items are attributed to Orr 'by style' in the trade; without a mark this is an attribution, not a reading.

facts.text: The V&A records 'ORR' stamped as a pseudo-hallmark on the back of a P. Orr & Sons spoon bowl of c.1876.
facts.quote: 'ORR' Stamped pseudo-hallmark on back of bowl of spoon, near the base of the stem

facts.text: Peter Orr's successor P. Orr & Sons 'continued the use of the "Orr" mark'.
facts.quote: Succeeded by P. Orr & Sons, the firm continued the use of the "Orr" mark.

facts.text: A dealer records 'ORR stamped to the side of the footed base' of a silver-gilt mug of c.1860.
A second V&A spoon (IS.49-2004, c.1876) carries 'ORR', described as the 'Pseudo-hallmark of P. Orr and Sons of Madras, stamped on the back of the bowl beneath the join with the stem'.
A cigar dish of c.1855 is stamped 'ORR', 'SILVER' and '9' on the base; the dealer states the firm marked its silver 'ORR' until about 1860 and 'P. Orr & Sons' afterwards.
facts.quote: ORR, SILVER and 9

rows.meaning: Maker's and retailer's mark of P. Orr & Sons, manufacturing jewelers, gold and silversmiths, Mount Road, Madras
rows.punch_set: Name and town in one punch; may be accompanied by a separate 'SILVER'

maker.name: P. Orr & Sons (later P. Orr & Sons Ltd)
maker.place: Mount Road, Madras; branch at Rangoon by 1918

rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.where_on_object: underside of hollowware; back of flatware
rows.date_note: P. Orr & Sons from 1860 (Wilkinson via 925-1000; an auction note says son James Edward Orr was apprenticed 1854 and made partner 1860) or 1863 (Michael Backman dealer text) - disputed; still listed as manufacturing silversmiths in 1924. Many sources give 1849 as the founding date of the business.
rows.what_it_tells: Madras-made (or Orr-retailed) silver, c.1860-1940s; Orr was the dominant maker of 'swami' silver and supplied royal and princely clients.
rows.cautions: Founding date disputed: 1849 (V&A, Grace's Guide/Whitaker 1914, firm catalogues), 1846 (VMFA, Wikipedia P.Orr & Sons), 1851 (Wilkinson via 925-1000 for Peter Orr's own shop). Orr also retailed imported English silver and electroplate; an Orr name on an item with British hallmarks marks the retailer, not the maker. Plain European-style Orr silver exists alongside swami work.

facts.text: P. Orr & Sons was established in Madras in 1849 and was the leading manufacturer of 'swami' work.
facts.quote: The leading manufacturer of "Swami" work was P. Orr and Sons of Madras

facts.text: In 1903 the firm claimed to be 'the pioneer manufacturing firm of India', with a Madras factory of upwards of 600 artisans, making jewelry, gold and silver ware and scientific instruments, with hand-chased swami silverware as a specialty.
facts.quote: Their factory at Madras, in which they employ upwards of 600 artizans, is reputed to be the largest and best appointed establishment of the kind in India.

facts.text: In 1914 the firm (head office Madras, London office Moorgate Station Chambers) described itself as manufacturing jewelers, goldsmiths, silversmiths and mathematical and surveying instrument makers, with about 1,000 employees.
The Asylum Press directories list P. Orr & Sons on Mount Road among Madras jewelers, gold and silversmiths in 1918 and 1924; by 1924 it was P. Orr & Sons Ltd with a branch at Rangoon.
facts.quote: ORR & SONS, LTD., P.— Post Box No. 117 [OCR], Madras; Branch, at Rangoon; Watch makers, Diamond Merchants, Manufacturing Jewellers, Silversmiths

facts.text: P. Orr and Sons were appointed 'Jewelers and Silversmiths to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales' in April 1876.
Marks recorded on Orr items include 'ORR & Sons, Madras', 'P. Orr & Sons of Madras' and 'ORR'.
A teapot of c.1890 is stamped 'P Orr & Sons/Madras' on the underside of the base.
facts.quote: The underside of the base is stamped 'P Orr & Sons/Madras'.

facts.text: Orr also made gold swami jewelry (V&A holds the fitted box for a gold swami bracelet by P. Orr & Sons, c.1875) and plain European-style silver (a plain tea set by Peter Orr & Sons, c.1900, sold 2026).
A two-line punch 'P. ORR & SONS / MADRAS' in a cut-cornered rectangle is illustrated for the firm.

rows.plain: P. Orr and Sons, Madras, Silver
variants: P Orr and Son Madras Silver
rows.meaning: Maker's name, town and metal statement of P. Orr & Sons, Madras
rows.punch_set: Three lines: firm name / MADRAS / SILVER
rows.technique: struck (incuse letters, no frame, in the photographed example)
rows.date_note: Seen on swami wares of c.1880 and later; exact first use not established.
rows.fineness: 'SILVER' is an unquantified claim; no assay or standard was applied in India before the 20th-century BIS scheme.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical later Orr mark on swami tea services and presentation items; the 'SILVER' word mirrors the practice of other Madras and Bangalore firms (Tawker, Krishniah Chetty, Barton).
rows.cautions: 'SILVER' is the maker's own claim, not an assay. A Bangalore-style item in the same sale was stamped by a Bombay retailer (Bhicajee & Co), so south Indian work can carry another city's retailer mark.

facts.text: A three-line incuse mark 'P. ORR & SONS / MADRAS / SILVER' is illustrated for P. Orr & Sons.
A three-piece swami bachelor's tea service by Peter Orr and Sons sold at Chiswick Auctions (2023) is 'marked P Orr and Son Madras Silver'; the design appears in a c.1880 Orr sales catalogue.
facts.quote: marked P Orr and Son Madras Silver

forms: P Orr and Son Madras Silver

rows.mark_text: T. R. TAWKER & SONS MADRAS SILVER
rows.plain: T. R. Tawker and Sons, Madras, Silver
variants: T. R. TAWKER & SONS with separate MADRAS town mark
rows.meaning: Maker's (or retailer's) mark of T. R. Tawker & Sons, jewelers, diamond merchants and silversmiths, Mount Road, Madras
rows.punch_set: Firm name, 'MADRAS' and 'SILVER' as separate words/punches on the underside or reverse

maker.name: T. R. Tawker & Sons
maker.place: Mount Road, Madras (family originally of Tiruchirappalli)

rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Firm headquarters moved to Madras by the mid-1890s; insolvency declared 17 January 1925. Marked items are catalogued c.1900-1910.
rows.fineness: 'SILVER' unquantified.
rows.what_it_tells: Swami and European-style silver from a leading Indian-owned Madras firm, c.1895-1925.
rows.cautions: A family firm of Gujarati origin; the 'T' in family names stands for Tiruchirappalli. Some dealer histories give a founding date of 1761 (unsupported); records of the family go back to 1759 (Nilakanta Tawker in Ananda Ranga Pillai's diary), not of the firm.

facts.text: Silver by T. R. Tawker & Sons is marked with the firm name, 'Madras' and 'Silver'.
facts.quote: T. R. TAWKER & SONS MADRAS SILVER

facts.text: At the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-3, T. R. Tawker and Sons of Mount Road, Madras, were described as manufacturing jewelers and silversmiths paying special attention to Indian jewelry; their display was valued at Rs 60,00,000.
facts.quote: They are manufacturing jewellers and silver-smiths who pay special attention to the subject of Indian jewellery.

facts.text: T. R. Tawker & Sons are listed on Mount Road among Madras jewelers, gold and silversmiths in 1918 and 1924.
The Tawkers declared insolvency on 17 January 1925 after mortgage litigation; their Mount Road showroom was designed by Henry Irwin.
Gopinatha Tawker (born 1862) was chief partner in 1908; the firm was founded by his father Ranganatha Tawker.

forms: T. R. TAWKER & SONS MADRAS SILVER

rows.meaning: Maker's or retailer's mark of Daday Khan, silversmith of Mount Road, Madras
rows.punch_set: Name with the 28 Mount Road, Madras address (reported by a dealer; exact wording, case and punch form not described)
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Exhibited at Delhi 1902-3; still listed among Madras jewelers in 1924. Dealer dates a marked tea set c.1880 (unverified).
rows.what_it_tells: Swami silver made in Madras by an Indian-owned workshop that rivaled Orr at the 1903 Delhi Exhibition.
rows.cautions: The exact form of the mark is recorded only by one dealer.

facts.text: Daday Khan of Mount Road, Madras, contributed a fine series of swami silver (punch bowls, claret jug, tea services) to the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-3 and won a third prize with bronze medal for a collection of silver plate.
facts.quote: A second and equally fine series is contributed by Daday Khan, of Mount Road, Madras

facts.text: Daday Khan, Mount Road, is listed among Madras jewelers, gold and silversmiths in 1924.
A swami tea set is described as 'Hallmarked Daday Khan, (28 Mount Road, Madras)'.
facts.quote: Hallmarked Daday Khan, (28 Mount Road, Madras)

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of C. Krishniah Chetty (& Sons), jewelers and silversmiths, Commercial Street, Bangalore
rows.punch_set: Name, 'BANGALORE' and 'SILVER' stamped on the base (transcribed by cataloguers in title case; exact letter case and line breaks not recorded)
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Firm founded 1869 (company history); marked swami silver is catalogued late 19th-early 20th century.
rows.fineness: 'SILVER' unquantified.
rows.what_it_tells: Bangalore swami silver from the leading Indian-owned Bangalore firm; exhibited at Delhi 1903 and jewelers to the Mysore court from 1910.
rows.cautions: The firm still trades (C. Krishniah Chetty Group); modern items and the jewelry brand 'CKC' are not antiques. Spellings Krishniah/Krishnaiah/Krishna refer to the same firm.

facts.text: Silver by C. Krishniah Chetty is stamped 'C. Krishniah Chetty Bangalore Silver' on the base (a jug and a four-piece tea service at Toovey's; a dealer's six-piece swami tea service 'hallmarked C. Krishniah Chetty, Bangalore').
facts.quote: stamped 'C. Krishniah Chetty Bangalore Silver' to base

facts.text: At the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-3 the best Bangalore swami silver (cups, punch bowls, vases) was by C. Krishniah Chetty, Jeweler of Bangalore, who also showed Calcutta (Bhowanipore)-style items and won a third prize.
facts.quote: all by C. Krishniah Chetty, Jeweller of Bangalore

facts.text: In 1924 Krishniah Chetty & Sons, C., of 162 Commercial Street, Bangalore, were listed as jewelers, silversmiths and diamond merchants.
The business was founded in 1869 by Cotha Krishniah Chetty in the Bangalore Cantonment and appointed jeweler to the Mysore court in 1910.

rows.meaning: Initials mark of C. Krishniah Chetty & Sons, Bangalore
rows.punch_set: Initials with '& SONS' and 'BANGALORE' (reported)
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Reported on items dated c.1890-1900 by a dealer.
rows.what_it_tells: Alternative mark of the Krishniah Chetty firm.
rows.cautions: Single dealer source; 'CKC' is also the firm's modern brand.

facts.text: A dealer records a 'Maker's mark CKC & Sons Bangalore' on Bangalore silver of c.1900.

variants: BARTON / BANGALORE with SILVER in a separate rectangular punch
rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Barton (Barton & Son(s)), silversmiths and jewelers, South Parade, Bangalore
rows.punch_set: 'BARTON BANGALORE' incuse in bold capitals, with 'SILVER' in a rectangular punch
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.where_on_object: outer rim of the base (one example)
rows.date_note: Barton arrived 1861; Orr & Barton from 1862; Barton alone after James Edward Orr retired in 1869. Marked example dated c.1890.
rows.fineness: 'SILVER' unquantified.
rows.what_it_tells: Bangalore-made silver, including swami work, from the European-owned Bangalore firm linked by marriage and partnership to the Orrs of Madras.
rows.cautions: The firm still trades in Bangalore (Barton Son & Co.), so modern items exist. The early partnership was 'Orr & Barton' (with James Edward Orr of the Madras family): marks of that period have not been recorded. 'BARTON' alone is ambiguous: Barton is a common English maker's name, and the Museum of Freemasonry catalogues a Madras district jewel stamped BARTON as made in England.

facts.text: Messrs. Barton & Sons of Bangalore showed four items of swami silver at the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-3, including a fruit stand modeled on the Nandi of Vellore temple.
facts.quote: Messrs. Barton & Sons of Bangalore have contributed four specimens in swami style

facts.text: A coconut cup of c.1890 is stamped 'BARTON BANGALORE' with 'SILVER' in a rectangular punch.
Thomas Barton arrived in India in 1861; with James Edward Orr he founded Orr and Barton by 1862; Orr retired in 1869 and Barton continued.
A Masonic jewel marked 'Barton' and 'Silver' is attributed by its owner to Barton of Bangalore.
The Museum of Freemasonry, London holds a collar jewel for a District Grand Superintendent of Works for Madras with 'BARTON' stamped on the back (catalogued with production place 'England').
facts.quote: 'BARTON' stamped on the back of the jewel

rows.meaning: Trade mark of Harrison Fisher & Co., Sheffield electroplate and cutlery makers - NOT a mark of Madras-made silver
rows.punch_set: 'MADRAS' and 'SILVER' in two adjoining rectangles
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.where_on_object: back of flatware stems; underside of hollowware
rows.date_note: Firm recorded at the British Industries Fair 1922 and 1947; years of use of the MADRAS SILVER trade mark not established.
rows.fineness: Usually a trade name for plated or white-metal wares; 'SILVER' here does not mean solid silver.
rows.what_it_tells: Sheffield-made plated or alloy flatware sold under a fancy trade name.
rows.cautions: Easily misread as 'silver from Madras'. Real Madras makers put their firm name before MADRAS (P. ORR & SONS MADRAS; T. R. TAWKER & SONS MADRAS). Check for British electroplate marks (EP, EPNS) and test the metal.

facts.text: Harrison Fisher & Co. of Sheffield used a mark reading 'MADRAS' and 'SILVER' in two rectangles.
facts.quote: | MADRAS || SILVER | inside two rectangles

facts.text: Harrison Fisher & Co., Trafalgar Works, Sheffield, made table cutlery, spoons and forks and electroplated ware (British Industries Fair 1922).

rows.meaning: Reported 20th-century mark read as ORR + SIL(ver) + a two-digit year number, attributed to P. Orr & Sons, Madras
rows.punch_set: Letters run together with a two-digit number (reported '60', '47')
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Forum participants read the numbers as years (e.g. 47 = 1947, 60 = 1960); one box also carries an inscription dated 1959.
rows.what_it_tells: If the reading is right, a late Orr mark that carries its own year number.
rows.cautions: Single forum discussion; attribution to Orr and the year reading are unconfirmed. Mostly after 1947.

facts.text: A plain box stamped 'ORRSIL60', with an inscription dated 1959, is read by collectors as ORR + SIL + year 60; other items reportedly carry '47' for 1947.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Oomersi Mawji of Bhuj, Kutch, court silversmith to the Maharao of Kutch; the same mark was used by the workshop his sons carried on (Oomersi Mawji & Sons).
rows.punch_set: Usually struck alone; 'O.M.' is sometimes found without the town name.

maker.name: Oomersi Mawji; from c. 1890 Oomersi Mawji & Sons

rows.technique: struck with a punch; LACMA records the letters as intaglio (sunk)
rows.date_note: Oomersi Mawji is said to have been active from c. 1860 (LACMA, V&A, Saffronart); his sons kept the workshop and the mark into the 1930s. Dated or datable marked items run c. 1870-1920. His own dates are disputed (see facts).
rows.fineness: The mark makes no claim. LACMA (Markel 2020), a Saffronart note and Pushkin's 2025 blog each say Kutch silver is 95-98 percent silver, but none cites a test; dealers' acid tests on marked O.M. items report '900+'. No legal standard applied.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the best-known Kutch workshop and the town (Bhuj). It cannot tell father's work from his sons', and it does not date the item within c. 1860-1930s.
rows.cautions: Most Kutch silver is unmarked, and many unmarked items are attributed to Oomersi Mawji on style alone; treat such attributions as opinions. Kutch-style ('Cutch') silver was also made in Bombay, Karachi and Lucknow and imitated by Tiffany, Gorham and Whiting, so the style is not proof of the maker. M.R. BHUJ is a different Bhuj maker. Items re-assayed in Britain may carry later British import marks alongside or instead of the original mark.

facts.text: The V&A's tea set by Oomersi Mawji is stamped OM; its water jug and sugar bowl are catalogued with the mark 'O.M. Bhuj' / 'O.M. BHUJ'.
facts.quote: All are stamped "OM", and are the work of the renowned Oomersi Mawji, Court Silversmith to the ruler of Kutch

facts.text: LACMA records the mark on its Oomersi Mawji and Sons mug as signed in intaglio 'O.M BHUJ' and says his and his sons' work is generally identifiable by a maker's mark stamped on the bottom.
facts.quote: his work and that of his sons is generally identifiable by a maker's mark stamped on the bottom

facts.text: Auction houses record the same mark as 'O.M BHUJ' (Bonhams 2014, box stamped on the underside) and 'O.M., Bhuj' or 'O.M.' (Saffronart 2012-2013).
facts.quote: Stamped on underside with maker's mark 'O.M BHUJ'

facts.text: Oomersi Mawji belonged to the Mochi (cobbler) caste; Baden-Powell (1894) calls him the best of the Cutch silversmiths and says the Mochis had earlier decorated armour plates. LACMA, citing Wilkinson 1999 p. 69, gives the same caste.
facts.quote: It is to this group the Umarsi Maoji, the best of the Cutch silversmiths, belongs.

facts.text: In 1879 the Bombay Gazetteer found the Cutch silver trade carried on only in Bhuj by very few families; of the leading men one was a shoemaker by caste (unnamed, consistent with Oomersi Mawji).
facts.quote: This industry is (1879) carried on only in Bhuj and there only by a very few families.

facts.text: He was court silversmith to Maharao Khengarji III of Kutch (r. 1875-1942).
His sons continued the workshop into the 1930s; one served as court silversmith to Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda.
facts.quote: Mawji's sons continued his workshop into the 1930s, with one serving as the court silversmith to Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III

facts.text: DISPUTED dates: LACMA and the V&A give him as active c. 1860-1890; Pushkin's 'Oomersi Mawji & Sons' page says he died c. 1890 and the firm ceased c. 1930; Pushkin's 2025 blog gives 1838-1910; a Bonhams 2021 footnote gives 'ca. 1860 - ca. 1930'.
Little Kutch silver was marked; the V&A says few items approached Oomersi Mawji's quality.
facts.quote: Little of this vast output was marked

facts.text: European customers bought Kutch silver through Bombay, where Cutch traders had agents; Bombay was the hub for making, selling and exporting Cutch-style silver.
facts.quote: it is through the latter that European customers are supplied with silver articles made in Cutch.

facts.text: Kutch silver was sold in London by Liberty & Co.
Several sources state Kutch silver is 95-98 percent silver (LACMA's catalogue gives 95-98 percent against sterling's 92.5); none of them cites an assay, and they may share an origin.
facts.quote: a very high standard of purity (95—98 percent silver compared to the minimum standard of 92.5 percent required for sterling silver)

facts.text: Dealers who acid-tested marked or attributed Kutch items report '900+' or '900 standard' rather than a figure.
Kutch silversmiths bought bar silver from Bania traders (1894) and their wares were sold by the rupee's weight of silver plus a charge (1879).
facts.quote: The workers employ bar silver, which they buy from the Bániya traders

facts.text: LACMA notes that American firms Tiffany, Whiting and Gorham made silver in the Kutch style.

rows.mark_text: Oomersee Mawjee / Silver Smith / Bhuj Cutch
rows.plain: Oomersee Mawjee, Silver Smith, Bhuj, Cutch
rows.meaning: Workshop name stamp of Oomersi Mawji (spelled Oomersee Mawjee) on a pencil design drawing from the Bhuj workshop.
rows.punch_set: On paper drawings, not on silver.
rows.technique: stamped on paper (ink or embossed not stated)
rows.date_note: Bonhams dates the drawing late 19th century; LACMA dates a related British Museum drawing late 19th-early 20th century, and Pushkin's 2025 blog mentions drawings on Dorling & Co. watermarked paper.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies a workshop design drawing, and shows the spelling the workshop itself used ('Oomersee Mawjee').
rows.cautions: Workshop drawings were made for clients to choose designs; a drawing does not prove a matching silver item was made by the workshop.

facts.text: A Bonhams pencil study for a mirror is stamped 'Oomersee Mawjee/Silver Smith/Bhuj Cutch'.
facts.quote: stamped Oomersee Mawjee/Silver Smith/Bhuj Cutch

facts.text: Oomersi Mawji spelled his name 'Mawjee' on his drawings and documents (Patel); a group of about three hundred workshop drawings was published by Dehejia in 2008.

forms: Oomersee Mawjee Silver Smith Bhuj Cutch

rows.meaning: Mark of the Oomersi Mawji family workshop at Baroda (Vadodara), used by a son working for the Gaekwad of Baroda.
rows.punch_set: Struck on the base of each item; one service had its original marks replaced by a Sheffield import mark in 1967 with only 'O.M. BARODA' still partly legible.

maker.name: son of Oomersi Mawji (named as Premjibhai by Patel; as 'Oomersee Mawji Jr.' by Pushkin)

rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Items are dated c. 1900-1930 by dealers; Sayajirao Gaekwad III ruled Baroda 1875-1939. Pushkin gives the maker as active 1920-1930.
rows.fineness: No claim in the mark; Patel notes the 1967 Sheffield import assay implies at least sterling for that service.
rows.what_it_tells: Places the item with the Baroda branch of the Oomersi Mawji family, early 20th century, rather than the Bhuj workshop.
rows.cautions: The son's name is not settled (Premjibhai per Patel; 'Oomersee Mawji Jr.' per Pushkin). Sources disagree on whether Oomersi Mawji himself served Baroda from the 1860s (Bonhams 2021, Pushkin) or only a son did (LACMA). Some Baroda items later received British import marks (F.D. for F. Drury Ltd, Sheffield, date letter Z = 1967) that replaced the original marks.

facts.text: A quail service by Premjibhai, son of Oomersi Mawji and court silversmith to Sayajirao Gaekwad III, is 'signed O.M•BARODA at the bottom of each item'.
facts.quote: signed “O.M•BARODA” at the bottom of each piece

facts.text: Pushkin records a scroll holder 'hallmarked O.M Baroda' for 'Oomersee Mawji Jr.', in the employment of the Gaekwad of Baroda.
facts.quote: Hallmarked 'O.M Baroda' for Oomersee Mawji Jr.

facts.text: One of Oomersi Mawji's sons served as court silversmith to Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda.
DISPUTED: Bonhams (2021) says the Maharajas of Baroda appointed Oomersi Mawji himself by 1860; Pushkin says he was court silversmith to Baroda in the 1860s.

rows.meaning: Name-and-town mark probably used by Oomersi Mawji's son working for the Gaekwad at Baroda in the early 20th century.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Bonhams and the British Museum (as cited by Bonhams) date the marked items early 20th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Same family as O.M. BHUJ and O.M. BARODA; places the item at Baroda in the early 20th century.
rows.cautions: Exact letter case and punctuation not published; catalogued only as 'Oomarsee Baroda'.

facts.text: A Bonhams bonbonniere is stamped 'Oomarsee Baroda' on the base; the same marks are on a British Museum salver (2011,3014.82) and were probably used by Oomersi Mawji's son working for the Gaekwar in Baroda.
facts.quote: The marks "Oomarsee Baroda" also appear on a salver in the British Museum dated to the early 20th Century

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of Mawji Raghavji (also written Raghavji Mawji), a Bhuj silversmith contemporary with Oomersi Mawji.
rows.punch_set: 'MR' and 'BHUJ', sometimes as two lines in one punch.
rows.technique: struck with a punch (described both as intaglio and as a 'cameo' punch)
rows.date_note: Marked items are dated c. 1880 by dealers and the Patel blog; years of activity not published.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies the second recorded named Bhuj maker; known also from design drawings with monumental and Hindu mythological subjects.
rows.cautions: DISPUTED name order: 'Mawji Raghavji' (Backman, Pushkin, Saffronart) vs 'Raghavji Mawji' (LACMA, Patel); the initials M.R. fit Mawji Raghavji. DISPUTED punch: Backman says stamped in intaglio; LACMA (citing Wilkinson 1999 fig. 139) calls it a 'cameo' punch. Relationship to Oomersi Mawji unknown.

facts.text: A Cutch jug of c. 1880 has its base stamped in intaglio with 'MR' and 'BHUJ', the maker's mark of Mawji Raghavji.
facts.quote: The base is stamped in intaglio with ‘MR’ and ‘BHUJ’.

facts.text: LACMA cites Wilkinson 1999, p. 90, fig. 139 for Raghavji Mawji's 'cameo' punch maker's mark 'M.R. | BHUJ' and calls him another leading Kutch artist.
facts.quote: For an illustration of Raghavji Mawji’s “cameo” punch maker’s mark, “M.R. | BHUJ”

facts.text: Patel records items 'stamped MR and BHUJ within inset rectangle', c. 1880, and calls him a contemporary of Oomersi who may or may not be related.
Pushkin lists 'M.R BHUJ' as the maker's mark for Mawji Raghavji.

rows.meaning: Mark of an unidentified Bhuj silversmith with the initials J.D.

maker.name: unidentified (possibly Jetha Dosa or Jaradi Davekur Kanji, per Wilkinson)

rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Items dated c. 1890 by the Patel blog.
rows.what_it_tells: A Bhuj-made item by a maker other than the Mawji workshops.
rows.cautions: Maker not identified; Wilkinson offers two candidates. Pushkin reports that 'Jaradi' is the family name of Oomersi Mawji's family, so a 'Jaradi' name does not by itself separate this maker from that family.

facts.text: Items marked 'Bhuj J.D.' are dated c. 1890; Wilkinson names Jetha Dosa and Jaradi Davekur Kanji as Kutch silversmiths whose mark this might be.
facts.quote: Wilkinson mentions two Kutch silversmiths whose mark this might be: Jetha Dosa and Jaradi Davekur Kanji.

rows.meaning: Initials of an unidentified Bhuj (Kutch) silversmith.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: c. 1890 per the dealer
rows.what_it_tells: Suggests a Bhuj maker other than Oomersi Mawji; identification not published.
rows.cautions: Reported only by one dealer; two-letter initials are common and the same letters could belong to makers elsewhere in India.

facts.text: A trophy cup c. 1890 (Bhuj region) is marked 'VK'; Pushkin cites Wilkinson, Indian Silver, p. 92 for the mark and reports an acid test of '900 standard'.

rows.meaning: Initials of an unidentified Bhuj (Kutch) silversmith.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: not stated
rows.what_it_tells: Suggests a Bhuj maker other than Oomersi Mawji; identification not published.
rows.cautions: Reported only by one dealer; two-letter initials are common and the same letters could belong to makers elsewhere in India.

facts.text: Pushkin's 2025 blog lists S.M among Bhuj silversmiths' identifying marks, with no further detail.

rows.meaning: Initials of an unidentified Bhuj (Kutch) silversmith.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: not stated
rows.what_it_tells: Suggests a Bhuj maker other than Oomersi Mawji; identification not published.
rows.cautions: Reported only by one dealer; two-letter initials are common and the same letters could belong to makers elsewhere in India.

facts.text: Pushkin's 2025 blog lists D.H among Bhuj silversmiths' identifying marks, with no further detail.

rows.plain: owner's name or initials engraved in Gujarati
rows.meaning: Gujarati-script letters engraved on Kutch silver usually name the owner, not the maker.
rows.punch_set: Found together with a struck maker's mark such as O.M. BHUJ, or on unmarked items.
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Date of the inscription can differ from the date of making.
rows.what_it_tells: May identify a Gujarati-speaking owner (for example a Kutch official) and support provenance.
rows.cautions: No Gujarati-script maker's mark on Kutch silver was found in any source: do not read Gujarati initials as a maker's mark. The exact Gujarati text of the two examples below is not published.

facts.text: An Oomersi Mawji box marked 'OM Bhuj' also bears Gujarati initials suggestive of the owner's name.
facts.quote: It also bears initials in Gujarati that is suggestive of the name of the owner.

facts.text: A Kutch tea cup is inscribed in Gujarati with the name 'Raja Motilal Lalbhai', the Diwan of Kutch (Diwan 1875-1902 per the provenance).
facts.quote: inscribed in Gujarati with the name 'Raja Motilal Lalbhai', the Diwan of Kutch

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of J. Manikrai (& Sons), a Kutch silversmith who re-established his workshop in Karachi after the 1899 Kutch famine.
rows.punch_set: Name, often with the touch mark 'T.95' and 'KARACHI' (Wilkinson 1999 p. 92), or with 'some pseudo hallmarks and the word silver' (Backman).
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Workshop moved to Karachi c. 1899; marked items dated c. 1900-1920 by dealers. End date unknown (1947 used only as an outer bound: Partition).
rows.fineness: Often with 'T.95', a self-applied claim of 95 percent silver; Pushkin reports acid tests of '900+'.
rows.what_it_tells: Kutch-style silver made in Karachi, Sind, c. 1900-1920s, not in Kutch itself.
rows.cautions: Karachi work closely follows Kutch designs and is easily mistaken for Bhuj work. DISPUTED: the 1909 Lahore silver medal is credited to J. Manikrai by Backman and Pushkin but to P. Manikrai by the Patel blog.

facts.text: Items are stamped on the base 'J Manikrai & Sons' with some pseudo hallmarks and the word 'silver'; the silversmith left Kutch c. 1899 for Karachi.
facts.quote: stamped to the base with ‘J Manikrai & Sons’ plus some pseudo hallmarks and the word ‘silver’

facts.text: Wilkinson (1999) p. 92 illustrates the mark 'J Manikrai' above 'T.95' above 'Karachi'.
facts.quote: one is J Manikrai, above T.95 above Karachi

facts.text: Patel records the hallmark 'J. Manikrai' on a Karachi tray c. 1900; Pushkin records items 'hallmarked J. Manikrai' with 'T95'.
Kutch silversmiths moved to Karachi after the 1899 famine in Kutch (Wilkinson 1999 as cited by Backman; Pushkin).
facts.quote: as a result of the 1899 famine in Kutch many silversmiths left Kutch and settled in Karachi

rows.meaning: Maker's mark of P. Manikrai, a Karachi silversmith formerly of Kutch.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: A crescent bowl is dated c. 1899.
rows.what_it_tells: Karachi-made Kutch-style silver, c. 1900.
rows.cautions: Relationship to J. Manikrai not established; the 1909 Lahore medal is credited to P. Manikrai here but to J. Manikrai by other sources.

facts.text: A crescent bowl c. 1899 bears the hallmark 'P. Manikrai', Karachi, formerly Kutch; silver medal, Indian Art Exhibition, Lahore, 1909.

rows.meaning: Maker's or retailer's mark of Soosania, Karachi.
rows.punch_set: Name above 'T.95' above 'Karachi'.
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Not published; the same mark layout as J. Manikrai suggests early 20th century.
rows.fineness: With 'T.95' (claimed 95 percent).
rows.what_it_tells: Karachi-made silver with a touch mark.
rows.cautions: Known only from Wilkinson 1999 p. 92 as reported on a collector forum; reading of the name not checked against the book.

facts.text: Wilkinson (1999) p. 92 shows the mark 'Soosania' above 'T.95' above 'Karachi'.
facts.quote: the second is Soosania, above T.95 above Karachi

rows.meaning: Self-applied purity mark on Kutch-style silver made in Bombay and Karachi: 'T' followed by the claimed silver content in percent (T.95 = 95 percent).
rows.punch_set: With a maker's name and town (e.g. J MANIKRAI / T.95 / KARACHI).
wares: Kutch-style silver made in Bombay and Karachi
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Karachi examples are dated c. 1900-1920 by dealers; a forum poster says the system was introduced c. 1920 (unsourced).
rows.fineness: Claims the stated percentage (T.100 to T.85 recorded). Not an assay-office mark; Pushkin reports a 'T95' set testing '900+'.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Bombay or Karachi manufacture in the early 20th century, and states the maker's own claim of fineness.
rows.cautions: Not an official hallmark. What 'T' stands for is not stated in the sources (a forum guess is 'tola percentage'); in the Indian bullion trade fineness was expressed as 'touch' (Mookerji 1905: '100 touch'), which would fit, but this is an interpretation. Do not confuse with modern BIS fineness numbers (925, 800) or with English 'sterling' marks. Bombay use of T marks belongs with the calcutta_bombay findings.

facts.text: Wilkinson (1999) states that some Bombay-made (and elsewhere) Cutch-style silver is marked T.100, T.95 or T.85 to indicate purity.
facts.quote: some bombay-made (and elsewhere) cutch-style silver is marked T.100, T.95 or T.85 intending to indicate the purity of silver

facts.text: Patel records Bombay items bearing 'T.100' to 'T.85' and a cup marked 'T.90'.

rows.meaning: Pictorial mark of a peacock struck under Lucknow silver; Lucknow smiths marked with animal, bird or flower devices, each the mark of one silversmith.
rows.punch_set: Usually the only mark.
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Marked items dated c. 1880-1900 by Bonhams and Patel.
rows.fineness: No claim. Charles (1905) reports it was said Lucknow silverware held less alloy than that of Delhi.
rows.what_it_tells: Suggests Lucknow manufacture, late 19th-early 20th century, by a particular (unnamed) smith.
rows.cautions: A dancing peacock is the mark normally found on Burmese silver (Bonhams), and Lucknow smiths copied Burmese silver and sometimes passed it off as old Burmese (Charles 1905): a peacock mark alone does not decide Burma vs Lucknow. Cross-reference the burma_ceylon findings.

facts.text: Lucknow items were marked on their undersides with animals, flowers or birds, each the mark of a particular silversmith; Patel records peacock marks on a tea service and a hunting bowl.

facts.text: In 1905 Lucknow silversmiths copied Burmese silver and, Charles suspected, sometimes blackened it to sell as old Burmese silver.

facts.text: Lucknow had practically a monopoly in the United Provinces of European-style silver (tea sets, toilet sets, vases, bowls), said to have been started in Ahiyaganj, Lucknow, by Hulchand and Munna Lal about fifty years before 1905.

rows.cautions: Attribution rests on Wilkinson 1999 as relayed by one dealer; an elephant alone is also a common Indian pseudo-hallmark device (e.g. Calcutta firms), so the tree matters.

facts.text: A Lucknow hunting bowl has an 'elephant and tree mark on underside', which Wilkinson attributes to a Lucknow maker found on items of consistently high quality.

facts.text: Patel records an elephant mark on a small Lucknow bowl c. 1890 (device not described further).

rows.meaning: Maker's initials of Maung Shwe Yon, master silversmith of Rangoon (died 1889), usually with a seated deer inside a star
rows.device: Seated or crouching deer inside a star. Owens describes a sixteen-point star; the V&A describes a six-pointed star on its bowl.
rows.punch_set: Letters M.S.Y. with the deer-in-star device on the underside. One bowl instead has 'MG SWE YON' and 'RANGOON' engraved inside an engraved sunburst.
rows.technique: punched and incised; also engraved
rows.date_note: Items with his own mark are attributed c. 1880-1889; he died in 1889. His sons kept the name and the deer device after 1889, so the deer alone does not date an item before 1889.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the leading Rangoon workshop of the 1880s. With the initials M.S.Y. alone the item is most likely from Maung Shwe Yon's own lifetime workshop; with 'BROS' it is from his sons' firm.
rows.cautions: The sons' firm (MSY Bros / Mg Shwe Yon Bros) used the same name and deer device, so a deer mark is not proof of a pre-1889 date. The star around the deer is described differently (six or sixteen points), so do not reject an item on the star count alone. The V&A records its M.S.Y. bowl as made at Sagaing, not Rangoon. Dealers sometimes call the deer a hare.

facts.text: Maung Shwe Yon was a Rangoon silversmith who died in 1889, shortly after completing a trophy for the Corps of Royal Engineers at Chatham.
facts.quote: he died in 1889 shortly after completing a 'splendid' trophy for the Corps of Royal Engineers at Chatham (Backman, paraphrasing Tilly 1902)

facts.text: His mark is the initials 'M.S.Y.' on the underside with a seated deer inside a star.
facts.quote: The bottom of the bowl is incised and punched with a six pointed star, a crouching deer, and the leters 'M.S.Y' (presumably the maker's mark). (V&A IM.6-1929)

facts.text: Owens describes the star as sixteen-pointed; the V&A describes the star on its bowl as six-pointed.
One bowl dated c. 1880 is engraved on the base with a sunburst containing 'MG SWE YON' and 'RANGOON'; 'MG' is the usual Burmese abbreviation for 'Maung'.
facts.quote: The base is engraved with a sun-burst in which the maker's name - 'MG SWE YON' and 'RANGOON' are engraved.

facts.text: H. L. Tilly (1902) called one of his pierced bowls the best example of this kind of work ever produced.
facts.quote: 'the best example of this kind of work ever produced' (Tilly 1902, quoted by Owens)

facts.text: The V&A gives Sagaing, Burma, late 19th century, as the place of making of its M.S.Y. water bowl.

rows.plain: Maung Shwe Yon Brothers, gold and silversmiths, Rangoon
rows.meaning: Firm mark of the sons of Maung Shwe Yon (Maung Shwe Bin, Maung Thu Hlaing, Maung Yin Maung), Godwin Road, Rangoon, after 1889
rows.device: Seated deer (the father's workshop device) struck with the name
rows.punch_set: Deer workshop mark with the firm's name and town in capitals
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Formed after the father's death in 1889; known as Mg Shwe Yon Bros from about 1899. Dated items of 1896 and 1899 and small bowls of c. 1905 are recorded. End date unknown.
rows.what_it_tells: The item comes from the sons' commercial firm in Rangoon, after 1889. Small bowls inscribed 'Mg. Shwe Yon Bros.' were made in some numbers around 1905.
rows.cautions: Shares the deer device and the Shwe Yon name with the father's own mark. No company records or catalogues are known to survive, so dates for particular marks rest on dated items.

facts.text: After Maung Shwe Yon's death in 1889 his three sons, Maung Shwe Bin, Maung Thu Hlaing and Maung Yin Maung, succeeded him.
facts.quote: Maung Shwe Yon died in 1889 and was succeeded by his three sons (Pushkin)

facts.text: The sons formed a firm called MSY Bros on Godwin Road, Rangoon; from about 1899 it was also known as Mg Shwe Yon Bros.
Bases are stamped with the deer workshop mark and 'MG.SHWE YON.BROS GOLD & SILVERSMITH RANGOON'.
facts.quote: stamped MG.SHWE YON.BROS GOLD & SILVERSMITH RANGOON

facts.text: Dated offering bowls of 1896 and 1899 are recorded, and small c. 1905 bowls are inscribed 'Mg. Shwe Yon Bros.'; no corporate records or catalogues are known to survive.
The deer mark continued after 1889: a bowl stamped with the deer mark of Maung Shwe Yon & Sons carries a presentation inscription dated 'Jany 1891-Decr 1896'.
facts.quote: Base stamped with the deer makers mark for Maung Shwe Yon & Sons, Rangoon. (Pushkin; both listings are from one dealer, so counted as one source)

rows.mark_text: MAUNG YIN MAUNG, MASTER SILVERSMITH, 29 GODWIN ROAD, RANGOON
rows.plain: Maung Yin Maung, master silversmith, 29 Godwin Road, Rangoon
rows.meaning: Signature of Maung Yin Maung, son of Maung Shwe Yon and the most praised Burmese silversmith of the early 20th century
rows.punch_set: Name, title and street address; one recorded bowl adds the year 1905
rows.technique: stamped or engraved (sources differ in wording)
rows.date_note: Dated and exhibited items span about 1899-1911 (Delhi 1902-03 gold medal; Rangoon 1904 prize; signed bowl 1905; Festival of Empire / Indian and Colonial Exhibition 1911). Working dates beyond these are not established.
rows.what_it_tells: A signed item by the leading Rangoon master of c. 1900-1911; the address dates it to his independent practice rather than to his father's workshop.
rows.cautions: Many of his works are unsigned. The V&A attributes its centrepiece IS.19-1971 to him only as 'probably' and records it as made in Mandalay, whereas Watt (1903) calls him 'of Rangoon'. He was also a partner in Mg Shwe Yon Bros, whose mark is different.

facts.text: At the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-03, Maung Yin Maung of Rangoon won First Prize with gold medal for a silver table center priced Rs. 1,000.
facts.quote: First Prize with gold medal to Maung Yin Maung of Rangoon for silver table centre, Rs. 1,000. (Watt 1903)

facts.text: A bowl of c. 1905 is inscribed with his name, his Rangoon address (29 Godwin Road) and the date 1905.
facts.quote: MAUNG YIN MAUNG, MASTER SILVERSMITH, 29 GODWIN ROAD, RANGOON (base stamp as quoted by Pushkin)

facts.text: He was one of the three sons who succeeded Maung Shwe Yon in 1889.
Many of his works are unsigned.
The V&A records its table centrepiece IS.19-1971 as 'probably Maung Yin Maung', made in Mandalay, late 19th century.
facts.quote: The centrepiece was probably made by Maung Yin Maung, who submitted a similar piece to the British Empire Exhibition in Delhi in 1902, for which he was awarded a gold medal.

forms: MAUNG YIN MAUNG, MASTER SILVERSMITH, 29 GODWIN ROAD, RANGOON

rows.punch_set: Initials alone on the base
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Attributed items are dated c. 1890-1905 by dealers and auction houses; the firm documentary date is his 1902-03 Delhi prize.
rows.what_it_tells: A Rangoon master whose bowl took a first prize at Delhi in 1902-03; his work is described as 'tapestry' style.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse with M.S.Y. (Maung Shwe Yon). Sources disagree slightly on his Delhi placing (first prize with silver medal per Watt; 'second only to Maung Yin Maung' per a dealer).

facts.text: Bowls by Maung Po Kin are marked on the underside with his initials 'M.P.K.'.
facts.quote: The underside marked with the elite silversmith Maung Po Kin's initials, "M.P.K." (Bonhams 2022)

facts.text: At the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-03 he received First Prize with silver medal for a bowl (No. 177), and two of his bowls (Nos. 177 and 200) were singled out from the Rangoon series.
facts.quote: First Prize with silver medal for bowl (No. 177), Rs. 399, by Maung Po Kin of Rangoon.

facts.text: His characteristic style is called 'tapestry'.

rows.mark_text: No 319 / Maung Hywet Nee / Latter Street / Rangoon
rows.plain: Maung Hywet Nee, Latter Street, Rangoon
rows.meaning: Signature and address of Maung Hywet Nee, late 19th-century silversmith of Moulmein and Rangoon
rows.punch_set: Number, name, street and town written in four lines
rows.technique: inscribed (written signature)
rows.date_note: Dealer dates the recorded bowl to the late 19th century and suggests it may have been shown at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition, London, 1886 (not confirmed).
rows.what_it_tells: An English-language signature with a number suggests an item made for an exhibition or a European client.
rows.cautions: Known from one dealer's account only. The same dealer reports other items signed in Burmese script; the form of that signature is not recorded.

facts.text: A late 19th-century pierced bowl is inscribed under the base 'No 319 / Maung Hywet Nee / Latter Street / Rangoon'.
facts.quote: The inscription to the underside of the bowl states:- No 319 Maung Hywet Nee Latter Street Rangoon

No 319 Maung Hywet Nee Latter Street
